question: Will cumulative additional US tariffs on eligible Indian-origin imports be ≥50% at 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-09-30
- On August 6, 2025, the President issued an Executive Order (EO) under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act imposing an additional ad valorem duty of 25% on imports that are products of India, citing India’s direct or indirect importation of Russian oil. The order specifies the rate, the effective timing, in-transit exceptions, and states that this duty applies in addition to other applicable duties (including those pursuant to EO 14257 when applicable). Implementing details were published by the Department of Homeland Security/U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) in the Federal Register on August 27, 2025. The notice created HTSUS heading 9903.01.84 providing “the duty provided in the applicable subheading +25%” for products of India, effective for entries at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time (EDT) on August 27, 2025, with specified vessel in-transit exceptions. The notice reiterates that the 25% duty is in addition to all other applicable duties and, when applicable, to duties imposed under EO 14257; it also enumerates exemptions via additional HTSUS headings (9903.01.85–.89). CBP’s Cargo Systems Messaging Service (CSMS) guidance to the trade on August 25, 2025 likewise instructs filers on applying the additional 25% under 9903.01.84, clarifies interaction with EO 14257 (reciprocal tariffs), lists exemptions (including the vessel in-transit exception via 9903.01.85), and confirms the effective date/time of 12:01 a.m. EDT on August 27, 2025.
- Separately, under EO 14257 (the reciprocal tariffs program), country-specific reciprocal tariff rates were established and later modified. As of July 31/August 6, 2025, India’s country-specific reciprocal tariff rate is 25%, implemented in HTSUS heading 9903.02.26, effective for entries for consumption on or after 12:01 a.m. EDT on August 7, 2025, subject to specified in-transit provisions and exclusions. This heading sets an additional ad valorem duty rate applicable to products of India under the reciprocal tariff framework. EO 14257 established the structure for reciprocal tariffs and exemptions (including Annex II lists) and provided that these ad valorem rates apply in addition to other applicable duties. The order also describes that the reciprocal tariffs generally apply to the non-U.S. content of a subject article and outlines broad exclusions in Annex II (e.g., certain Section 232-covered goods and specified categories like pharmaceuticals and certain critical minerals). The published EO text does not itself include the India-specific percentage within its body; those country rates are supplied via subsequent implementing and modifying actions/annexes.
- Together, these measures mean that, for eligible Indian-origin goods to which both HTSUS 9903.02.26 (reciprocal tariff, 25%) and 9903.01.84 (India IEEPA tariff, 25%) apply (i.e., goods not covered by specified exclusions), the combined additional ad valorem duty is 50%. The Federal Register implementation for the India IEEPA tariff explicitly states that the 25% applies in addition to duties under EO 14257 when applicable , and CBP’s CSMS guidance likewise indicates stacking.

Key definitions and context
- Additional ad valorem duty: An additional percentage charge assessed on the customs value of an imported article, on top of the preexisting duty rate(s). See general definition of ad valorem tax/duty: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad_valorem_tax
- HTSUS: The Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States, which codifies tariff provisions, including Chapter 99 temporary/additional duties. See: https://hts.usitc.gov
- Products of India: Country of origin determined under U.S. customs rules (e.g., substantial transformation). For this market question, the relevant operative texts use the phrase “articles/products of India” and apply country-of-origin tests accordingly [636d6d; 1ced9b; 5f17de].
- Effective times and time zones: The 25% IEEPA duty on products of India took effect for entries for consumption on or after 12:01 a.m. EDT on August 27, 2025 [636d6d; 1ced9b]. India’s reciprocal tariff rate of 25% was effective for entries for consumption on or after 12:01 a.m. EDT on August 7, 2025. This forecasting market resolves using UTC; conversions are not needed for background but are specified in the resolution criteria below.
- Exemptions/exclusions: The India IEEPA notice lists specific exemptions (e.g., HTSUS 9903.01.85 in-transit vessel shipments with cutoffs, informational materials, donations to relieve human suffering, certain 232-covered categories, etc.) [636d6d; 1ced9b]. EO 14257’s framework (and subsequent modifications) provides Annex II exclusions and describes the reciprocal tariff applying generally to non-U.S. content and in addition to other duties.
- Modification authority: The India IEEPA EO contains explicit modification authority allowing the President to adjust or terminate the measure in light of changed circumstances or retaliatory actions. This creates genuine uncertainty about whether the combined additional duty burden will remain at least 50% by year-end.

Why this is forecastable and non-trivial
- As of 2025-09-30, both the 25% India IEEPA duty and the 25% India reciprocal duty are in force, creating a 50% combined additional duty for eligible goods [636d6d; 1ced9b; 5266ed; 359c91; 5f17de]. Future administrative actions could suspend, reduce, or modify one or both measures, or expand exclusions, making the end-of-year status uncertain. Forecasters can track Federal Register notices, CBP CSMS updates, and White House actions for changes.
resolution_criteria:
Question
- Resolve to Yes if, at 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, both of the following are in effect for entries for consumption of products of India (country of origin India) such that they concurrently apply to eligible entries: (a) an additional 25% ad valorem duty under HTSUS heading 9903.01.84 (or its direct legal successor implementing EO 14329’s India-specific IEEPA duty), and (b) an additional 25% ad valorem duty under the India-specific reciprocal tariff heading (HTSUS 9903.02.26 or any renumbered successor) implementing EO 14257 and its modifications. If both are in effect at that time, the cumulative additional ad valorem duty burden is deemed to be ≥50% for eligible goods.
- Resolve to No otherwise (e.g., if either heading is not in effect, suspended, or reduced such that the combined additional ad valorem rate that would concurrently apply to eligible entries is <50%).

Definitions
- In effect: Legally operative for entries for consumption at the resolution timestamp (23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025). Evidence includes active Federal Register notices/orders and CBP operational guidance indicating collection, without a stay/injunction suspending collection nationwide.
- Eligible entries/goods: Articles that are products of India (country of origin India) entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, at or after the resolution timestamp, that are not excluded by the specific exemptions listed in the operative texts (e.g., HTSUS 9903.01.85–.89 for the India IEEPA duty; Annex II exclusions or other specified exceptions for the reciprocal tariff under EO 14257 and its modifications). Stated differently, “eligible” means goods for which both headings would apply concurrently under their own terms [636d6d; 1ced9b; 359c91].
- Additional ad valorem duty: An added percentage of customs value assessed under HTSUS Chapter 99 headings (e.g., 9903.01.84, 9903.02.26) in addition to base MFN rates and any other applicable duties; see general definition at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad_valorem_tax. The India IEEPA notice explicitly states stacking with other applicable duties, including EO 14257 when applicable , and CBP CSMS reiterates this.

Scope and date range
- Start date: 00:00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025. End/resolution timestamp: 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. The market resolves based on the legal status at the resolution timestamp; interim changes do not affect resolution unless they are in effect at the timestamp.

Primary resolution sources (authority order)
1) Federal Register: Notices, executive orders, and amendments that implement, suspend, or modify HTSUS headings 9903.01.84 and 9903.02.26 (or direct successors) [636d6d; 5266ed; 359c91; 5f17de].
2) CBP CSMS and official CBP webpages providing operational guidance on collection/suspension as of the resolution timestamp.
3) As needed, the White House presidential actions page for relevant executive orders or memoranda [5f17de; 359c91].

How to adjudicate
- YES: Adjudicators find, as of the resolution timestamp, that 9903.01.84 remains active at +25% for products of India and that an India-specific reciprocal tariff heading remains active at +25% (e.g., 9903.02.26), with no effective suspension/termination that would prevent both from applying concurrently to eligible entries. The Federal Register India implementation notice explicitly provides that the 25% IEEPA duty applies in addition to EO 14257 duties when applicable , and CBP CSMS confirms concurrent application.
- NO: Adjudicators find that either (i) 9903.01.84 has been rescinded, suspended, or reduced below 25%, or (ii) the India reciprocal heading (e.g., 9903.02.26) has been rescinded, suspended, or reduced below 25%, or (iii) an authoritative notice makes clear that both cannot concurrently apply to any eligible entries at the resolution timestamp, resulting in a combined additional rate <50%.

Tie-breakers and conflicts
- If sources conflict, Federal Register publications control. If an operative measure is enjoined nationwide and CBP has issued instructions to suspend collection as of the resolution timestamp, treat that measure as not in effect for purposes of this market [636d6d; 1ced9b].

Citations to establish baseline status
- EO imposing the 25% additional duty on products of India (legal authority, scope, effective timing, modification authority).
- Federal Register notice implementing the India 25% duty in HTSUS 9903.01.84; effective time, in-transit exception; explicit stacking with EO 14257 when applicable; exemptions listed.
- CBP CSMS guidance on applying 9903.01.84; effective time; stacking; exemptions; filer instructions.
- EO 14257 framework for reciprocal tariffs; exclusions and structure; note that country-specific rates are provided via subsequent annexes/updates.
- India’s reciprocal tariff rate of 25% and HTSUS heading 9903.02.26; effective timing and exclusions.

question: Will the EU adopt a legal act by December 31, 2025 that postpones the EUDR’s general entry into application for non‑SME operators and traders beyond December 30, 2025?
background:
Context and current status as of 2025-09-30:
- What is the EUDR: Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 of 31 May 2023 on making available on the Union market and exporting certain commodities and products associated with deforestation and forest degradation (repealing Regulation (EU) No 995/2010). It sets due‑diligence obligations for EU ‘operators’ and ‘traders’ placing or exporting relevant products (e.g., cattle, cocoa, coffee, palm oil, rubber, soy, wood).
- Key definitions in the Regulation: ‘Operator’ means any natural or legal person who, in the course of a commercial activity, places relevant products on the market or exports them; ‘Trader’ means any person in the supply chain other than the operator who, in the course of a commercial activity, makes relevant products available on the market.
- Timeline to date: The EUDR entered into force on 29 June 2023. Following an additional 12‑month phasing‑in granted in December 2024, most obligations for operators and traders apply from 30 December 2025 for large and medium companies, and from 30 June 2026 for micro‑ and small‑undertakings (as defined under Directive 2013/34/EU). These timeline clarifications are set out in the Commission’s August 12, 2025 Guidance Document and on the official Commission ‘Environment’ page.
- Information System: The EUDR Information System (for submission of due diligence statements) was launched on 4 December 2024; registration opened in November 2024. The Guidance Document details how operators/traders use the system and underlines it is equipped with security and data‑protection safeguards.
- Current policy signal: On September 23, 2025, the European Commission publicly stated that the EU would delay launching the EUDR for another year due to concerns about the readiness and load capacity of the IT system supporting the law. Reuters reports the announcement and notes the postponement would require approval by the European Parliament and EU Member States (Council).
Why this question is non‑trivial: A further postponement would likely require an adopted EU legal act amending application dates for the core obligations (Articles 3–13, 16–24, 26, 31, 32). The Commission has signaled intent, but adoption by co‑legislators is uncertain and time‑bound. Forecasters should consider legislative dynamics, institutional capacity, stakeholder pressure, and IT readiness. The result should be clearly knowable by year‑end using official sources.
resolution_criteria:
Event window and timezone:
- Eligible events must occur between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

What counts as a ‘postponement’ for this question:
- ‘Entry into application’ refers to the date when most obligations on operators and traders (including Articles 3–13, 16–24, 26, 31, 32) become applicable. As clarified by the Commission Guidance, these apply from 30 December 2025 for non‑SME operators and traders (large and medium companies), and from 30 June 2026 for micro‑ and small‑undertakings.
- For the purposes of this market question, a ‘postponement’ is a change to the general application date for non‑SME operators and traders (currently 2025-12-30) to any later date (i.e., a calendar date after 2025-12-30). Changes that only affect SMEs or only specific sectors/products do not count unless they also postpone the general non‑SME application date.

Resolve ‘Yes’ if, by the deadline above, the European Union has adopted a binding legal act that sets the general application date for non‑SME operators and traders under Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 to a date later than 2025-12-30. Acceptable proof includes any one of:
1) An amending Regulation (adopted by the European Parliament and the Council) published in the Official Journal (OJ L) and appearing on EUR‑Lex, that explicitly modifies the EUDR’s application date beyond 2025-12-30.
2) The EUR‑Lex consolidated text of 32023R1115 reflecting an amendment to Articles governing application dates (e.g., Articles 37–38) that moves the non‑SME application date beyond 2025-12-30.
3) If OJ publication is pending but adoption is confirmed by official institutional communications dated within the event window: a Commission press release (‘Press corner’), plus a matching confirmation from either the European Parliament (News/Press) or the Council (Press), all explicitly stating that the amending Regulation has been adopted and specifying the new later application date. Note: Mere proposals, political agreements without formal adoption, or general communiqués lacking the exact new date do not suffice.

Resolve ‘No’ if, by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, none of the above proof conditions are met. In particular, resolve ‘No’ if only an intention or proposal to postpone exists without formal adoption; or if any adopted act does not move the general non‑SME application date beyond 2025‑12‑30.

Definitions for resolvability:
- EUDR: Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 (‘Regulation on deforestation‑free products’), as published on EUR‑Lex.
- Operator: As defined in Article 2(15) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1115.
- Trader: As defined in Article 2(17) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1115.
- Non‑SME operator/trader: Large or medium companies; SMEs are micro‑ or small‑undertakings per Directive 2013/34/EU; the Commission Guidance applies deferred application to SMEs until 2026-06-30.
- Entry into application: The date from which most obligations apply; as of now, 2025-12-30 for non‑SMEs, per Commission Guidance and Commission website.

Primary resolution sources:
- EUR‑Lex (Official Journal entries for amending acts; consolidated text of 32023R1115). Example core text reference: Regulation (EU) 2023/1115.
- Official Journal of the European Union (OJ L) entries, accessible via EUR‑Lex.
- Official institutional press communications: European Commission Press corner; European Parliament News; Council press releases—only to confirm adoption and the new date if OJ publication lags, not for mere proposals.

Notes:
- Background and definitions cite the Commission Guidance Document (12 Aug 2025) and the Commission’s Environment page for current application dates and phasing‑in; Reuters reporting evidences the Commission’s stated intention and institutional approval requirement as of late September 2025.

question: Euro area flash HICP for November 2025 ≥ 2.3% year-over-year?
background:
Summary of what’s being forecast
- This question asks whether the euro area’s flash estimate of annual inflation (the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, HICP, all-items) for November 2025 will be at least 2.3% year-over-year (YoY).

Key definitions and scope (with authoritative sources)
- Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP): Eurostat’s harmonised consumer price index measuring the change over time in prices of consumer goods and services acquired by households in monetary transactions. It is compiled using harmonised concepts, methods and procedures across EU countries to ensure comparability. HICP indices are published monthly and used to calculate monthly and annual rates of change. See: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Consumer_prices_-_inflation and https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/prc_hicp_esms.htm
- Flash estimate: An early estimate of the euro area HICP annual inflation rate published monthly, usually on the last working day of the reference month (e.g., the November flash is typically at end-November). It is later replaced by the full monthly release in the middle of the following month. Differences between the flash estimate and the subsequent monthly HICP are not considered “revisions” of the flash figure; they are separate publications.
- Euro area (a.k.a. eurozone): The group of EU Member States that have adopted the euro as their single currency. As of 1 January 2023, Croatia joined as the 20th member, so the euro area comprises 20 countries (and this remains the case in 2025). See: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Glossary:Euro_area
- Annual (YoY) rate in this context means the year-over-year percentage change for the all-items HICP for the euro area aggregate, as published by Eurostat (i.e., the “annual inflation” headline rate in the flash estimate news release).

Where the number comes from and publication cadence
- Eurostat publishes the euro area inflation flash estimate as a “Euro indicators” news release, on its Eurostat website, following a pre-announced monthly calendar. The flash is typically at the end of the reference month; a full monthly release follows in the middle of the next month. See: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/news/euro-indicators

Status quo as of 2025-10-01 (context for forecasters)
- Recent readings in 2025 have been near the European Central Bank’s 2% objective. For August 2025, Eurostat’s flash estimate was 2.1% YoY (published 2 September 2025) , while the final euro area annual inflation rate for August 2025 was 2.0% (published 17 September 2025).
- Component contributions in August 2025 (final): services contributed +1.44 percentage points (pp), food/alcohol/tobacco +0.62 pp, non-energy industrial goods +0.18 pp, while energy contributed -0.19 pp. These illustrate current drivers and headwinds into late 2025. 

Why this threshold/date window
- The 2.3% threshold sits close to recent outcomes (2.0–2.1% in August 2025 flash/final), creating non-trivial uncertainty for November given energy base effects and services/core dynamics. The flash estimate for November 2025 is expected to be released before year-end based on Eurostat’s long-standing practice of publishing the flash at the end of each reference month (and doing so monthly since 2001).
resolution_criteria:
- Forecasted proposition: Resolve YES if the euro area’s flash estimate of annual inflation (all-items HICP) for November 2025, as published by Eurostat, is greater than or equal to 2.3% (YoY). Resolve NO if it is less than 2.3%.

- What exactly is measured:
  • Use the “annual inflation” (year-over-year) percentage for the all-items HICP aggregate for the euro area (EA20) as stated in Eurostat’s flash estimate news release for November 2025. This is the headline YoY rate in the flash estimate and refers to the euro area as defined by Eurostat (EU Member States that adopted the euro; 20 members as of 2025).

- Eligible time window and version control (times in UTC):
  • Eligible source publication must appear between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC on Eurostat’s website.
  • Use the first flash estimate news release for “Euro area annual inflation … November 2025” posted by Eurostat within this window. If Eurostat issues a correction to the flash estimate within 24 hours of the initial publication, use the corrected figure; otherwise, use the figure from the first flash estimate news release.

- Source of truth (single source):
  • Eurostat’s “Euro indicators” news release announcing the flash estimate for euro area inflation for November 2025 (e.g., on https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/news/euro-indicators). This page is where Eurostat routinely publishes monthly flash estimate press releases for euro area inflation. The flash estimate is typically published at the end of the reference month and precedes the full monthly release in mid-month.

- Disambiguations and exclusions:
  • Use euro area (EA) aggregate, not EU aggregate.
  • Use all-items HICP, not core HICP and not month-over-month or 12‑month moving average rates.
  • Use the flash estimate publication; do not substitute the later full monthly release. Differences between the flash estimate and monthly HICP are not treated as revisions of the flash value.

- Verification: A resolver should navigate to Eurostat’s Euro indicators page, open the November 2025 inflation flash estimate news release, and read the headline annual inflation (YoY) percentage for the euro area. If that value is ≥ 2.3%, resolve YES; otherwise, resolve NO.

question: Will Russia enact, extend, or broaden any nationwide legal ban on exports of motor gasoline or diesel fuel between 00:00 UTC Oct 15 and 23:59 UTC Dec 31, 2025?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: Russia has extended a nationwide ban on motor gasoline exports until Dec 31, 2025, and imposed a partial ban on diesel exports (applying to resellers/traders, not direct producers), according to government statements reported by Reuters and TASS. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed on Oct 1 that the government had extended gasoline export restrictions until year-end and introduced a diesel export ban for traders, while stating the domestic supply situation was being addressed and export markets could reopen if supply exceeds demand. These measures followed sustained Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian energy infrastructure which reduced refining by almost a fifth on certain days and cut exports from key ports , including incidents at the Afipsky refinery in late August and again on Sept 26, 2025.

Definitions and scope:
- Motor gasoline (petrol): a petroleum-derived fuel used in spark-ignition engines, formulated as a motor fuel.
- Diesel fuel (also termed diesel oil or gas oil): a liquid fuel for compression-ignition (diesel) engines; the common type is a petroleum distillate; “gas oil” is sometimes used interchangeably with diesel fuel.
- Nationwide legal ban on exports: a prohibition enacted via a federal government legal act (e.g., decree/resolution) that suspends or forbids the export of the specified fuel types outside the Russian Federation, applicable across the country. TASS reporting on the Sept 30, 2025 Cabinet decree explicitly described a ban on motor gasoline exports “outside the country” until Dec 31, 2025, and a separate decree banning exports of diesel, marine fuel oil, and other gasoils purchased on exchange, with exemptions for direct producers.
- Federal government legal act: an official normative legal act (e.g., “postanovlenie” or “rasporyazhenie”) published on Russia’s Official Internet Portal of Legal Information (pravo.gov.ru), which is the official source for the text of legal acts.
- Producers vs resellers/traders: consistent with Russian government and state media descriptions, “producers” are entities that manufacture the fuel; “resellers/traders” are entities that export fuel they did not produce themselves (e.g., purchased via exchanges). Sept 30 reporting distinguishes bans by exporter category.

Why this question is plausible and uncertain: While current bans run through end-2025, authorities have signaled that further restrictions are possible if needed, and the fuel market remains sensitive to refinery outages and security incidents, creating genuine uncertainty about whether Moscow will enact new measures or extend/broaden existing ones during Oct–Dec 2025.

Primary resolution sources: Official publications on the Russian government’s legal portal (http://pravo.gov.ru). If needed for verification, contemporaneous reporting by credible outlets such as Reuters and TASS will be used.
resolution_criteria:
This resolves to Yes if, between 00:00 UTC on Oct 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on Dec 31, 2025, at least one new nationwide legal ban or a formal extension/expansion of an existing ban on exports of motor gasoline or diesel fuel is enacted by the Russian federal government and published on its official legal portal (pravo.gov.ru) , or is clearly confirmed by credible contemporaneous reporting such as Reuters or TASS. Otherwise, the resolution is No.

Operational definitions and tests:
- Eligible action: A federal government legal act (e.g., decree/resolution) that (a) newly imposes an export ban on motor gasoline or diesel fuel (as defined) that was not in force for the affected exporter category or product as of 00:00 UTC on Oct 15, 2025; or (b) formally extends the expiration date of any such export ban beyond its prior end date; or (c) broadens the scope of an existing export ban by adding fuel products within the definitions above or expanding covered exporter categories (e.g., extending a diesel ban from resellers/traders to include producers). TASS and Reuters reporting on Sept 30, 2025 exemplify the types of acts and distinctions by exporter category.
- In-scope fuels: Motor gasoline (petrol)  and diesel fuel/gas oil. If a legal act references “gas oil” or “diesel fuel,” it counts under diesel; if it references “motor gasoline,” it counts under gasoline. Acts exclusively covering other petroleum products (e.g., crude oil) do not count.
- Nationwide: The measure must be federal and applicable across the Russian Federation; regional or local restrictions do not count.
- Evidence required: A URL to the promulgated act on pravo.gov.ru  (or an official government site hosting the text) is sufficient. If the legal text is not immediately available, two credible reports from Reuters and/or TASS confirming the act’s enactment and scope are acceptable.
- Time standard: Eligibility is based on the date-time of promulgation/publication of the act (or the date-time of the government’s official notice) in UTC. Acts promulgated before 00:00 UTC on Oct 15, 2025, or after 23:59 UTC on Dec 31, 2025, do not count.
- Non-qualifying actions: Non-binding statements, policy discussions, price controls, rationing, internal distribution measures, or administrative adjustments that do not constitute a formal export ban on the specified fuels are out of scope.

Resolution notes: The resolver will search pravo.gov.ru for relevant decrees during the specified window , and cross-check with Reuters/TASS coverage if necessary. Context about current bans and the refinery situation is provided for forecasters’ background.

question: U.S. core PCE year-over-year for November 2025 ≥ 2.8%?
background:
Definitions and measurement:
- Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index excluding food and energy ("core PCE"): A measure of prices paid by consumers for goods and services that omits food and energy to better reflect underlying inflation. BEA describes this series and its purpose on its data page and FAQ.
- Year-over-year (YoY) in BEA releases corresponds to the "12-month percent change" and is also presented as "Change from one year ago" in tables and bullets. This is the metric used for both the overall PCE price index and the core PCE index in monthly Personal Income and Outlays releases.

Release timing and source:
- The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) schedules "Personal Income and Outlays, November 2025" for December 19, 2025 at 10:00 AM; this monthly release contains the PCE price indexes and their 12-month percent changes. This BEA release page and its accompanying tables will be the primary source for resolution.

Status quo as of today (2025-10-01):
- In the latest available BEA release (August 2025), the 12-month percent change was 2.7% for the overall PCE price index and 2.9% for the PCE price index excluding food and energy (core). These values are stated in the August 2025 Personal Income and Outlays news release.
- The BEA core PCE data page currently shows recent "Change From Month One Year Ago" values for the core index of +2.9% (August 2025), +2.9% (July 2025), and +2.8% (June 2025).

Why this question:
- Core PCE YoY near year-end 2025 is policy-relevant and plausibly uncertain. The recent readings around 2.8–2.9% suggest meaningful two-sided risk for November 2025, making a 2.8% threshold non-trivial.

Eligible timeframe for forecasting context events (not for resolution data):
- Any contextual developments a forecaster considers may occur between October 15, 2025 00:00 UTC and December 31, 2025 23:59 UTC. Resolution itself will rely solely on the BEA publication referenced above.
resolution_criteria:
Resolve YES if the BEA "Personal Income and Outlays, November 2025" release lists the PCE price index excluding food and energy (core PCE) 12-month percent change (a.k.a. "From one year ago") for November 2025 as 2.8% or higher; resolve NO otherwise.

Operational details:
- Source of truth: The BEA news release page for "Personal Income and Outlays, November 2025" and/or the accompanying data tables posted with that release on bea.gov. The BEA core PCE data page (PCE price index excluding food and energy) is acceptable if it displays the November 2025 "Change From Month One Year Ago" value contemporaneously with the release.
- Use the first value published on the release date (December 19, 2025) for resolution. Subsequent revisions will not affect resolution.
- Use the percentage as published by BEA (to the precision they report; typically one decimal place). For avoidance of doubt: a published value of 2.8% counts as "2.8% or higher".
- Timezone for the resolution deadline: The question will be considered resolved as soon as the BEA release is published; if needed for administrative closure, the final deadline is December 31, 2025 at 23:59 UTC, but the value used is the one first published on December 19, 2025.

Key term references for adjudication:
- Core PCE definition (BEA): "personal consumption expenditures (PCE) prices excluding food and energy prices".
- BEA core PCE data page and its "Change From Month One Year Ago" presentation.
- Example of BEA release format showing 12-month percent change figures (August 2025 news release).

question: Will a U.S. Act of Congress enacted between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025 rescind at least $2.0 billion in budget authority?
background:
Definitions and legal context as of Sep 30, 2025:
- Rescission (Impoundment Control Act context): GAO describes a rescission as the proposed cancellation of budget authority before that authority would otherwise expire, initiated via a presidential special message to Congress under the Impoundment Control Act (ICA). Congress must enact a rescission into law for the cancellation to take effect; otherwise the funds must be made available after the ICA’s time limits. ICA’s rescission procedure is codified at 2 U.S.C. § 683 (special messages and the 45-day continuous session rule).
- Budget authority: GAO defines budget authority as authority provided by federal law to enter into financial obligations that will result in immediate or future outlays of federal funds.
- Counting rescissions (definiteness rule): GAO guidance on rescission statistics indicates that rescissions comprising indefinite or uncertain amounts (e.g., “up to” or “not more than”) are not counted; if a law rescinds “not less than” a specific amount, that minimum can be counted; otherwise only definite amounts are included.

Status quo and recent activity:
- On May 28, 2025, the Administration transmitted a special message proposing approximately $9.4 billion in rescissions of budget authority.
- Congress subsequently enacted the Rescissions Act of 2025 as Public Law 119-28 on July 24, 2025, rescinding specified budget authority in multiple accounts (as reflected on Congress.gov’s public law page for H.R.4).
- On August 28, 2025, the Administration transmitted another special message proposing rescissions totaling $4,999,999,990 across various foreign assistance and international organization accounts. The White House characterized this late-August package as a “pocket rescission” totaling $5 billion near the end of the fiscal year. GAO has explained that “pocket rescissions” (withholding proposed rescissions until funds expire near FY-end) are illegal under the ICA because the Act does not permit withholding through expiration absent congressional action.

Why this matters for forecasting: A second-half‑2025 attempt to cancel billions in previously appropriated funds has created uncertainty about whether Congress will enact another significant rescission by year‑end. The ICA provides a pathway but also constrains timing. Political dynamics around foreign aid, public broadcasting, and separation-of-powers disputes add further uncertainty.

Useful references (for forecasters and resolvers):
- GAO ICA explainer: https://www.gao.gov/legal/appropriations-law/impoundment-control-act 
- Statute: 2 U.S.C. § 683 (LII): https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/2/683 
- GAO Glossary (budget authority definition excerpted): https://www.gao.gov/assets/a76916.html 
- GAO rescission counting note: https://www.gao.gov/products/b-330828 
- May 28, 2025 special message (~$9.4B): https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Proposed-Rescissions-of-Budgetary-Resources.pdf 
- H.R.4 public law page (example of how Congress.gov displays enacted rescissions): https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/4 
- Aug 28, 2025 special message (~$5.0B): https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Proposed-Rescissions-of-Budgetary-Resources-August-28-2025.pdf 
- White House “pocket rescission” press statement (late Aug 2025): https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2025/08/historic-pocket-rescission-package-eliminates-woke-weaponized-and-wasteful-spending/ 
- GAO blog on pocket rescissions’ illegality: https://www.gao.gov/blog/what-pocket-rescission-and-it-legal
resolution_criteria:
Question: Will at least one U.S. federal law enacted between Oct 15, 2025 00:00:00 UTC and Dec 31, 2025 23:59:59 UTC rescind (i.e., cancel via enacted legislation) definite amounts of budget authority totaling ≥ $2,000,000,000 (two billion U.S. dollars, nominal)?

Definitions for this question:
- “Rescinds” means enacted legislation that cancels previously provided budget authority, consistent with the ICA framework for rescission proposals and congressional enactment into law.
- “Budget authority” is as defined by GAO: authority provided by law to enter into obligations that will result in immediate or future outlays of federal funds.
- “Definite amounts” follow GAO’s counting guidance: only definite, specified dollar amounts in the law’s text count toward the total; amounts phrased as “up to,” “not more than,” or other indefinite formulations do not count. If the law rescinds “not less than” a specific amount, count that minimum amount.
- “U.S. federal law enacted” means a bill or joint resolution that has become a Public Law during the window, whether by presidential signature or congressional veto override, with an official enactment date within the window (as displayed on Congress.gov). The enactment date governs, not the effective date. Public Law format example and status display: Congress.gov page for Public Law 119-28 (H.R.4).
- “Totaling ≥ $2,000,000,000” means the sum of all definite rescinded amounts specified within a single enacted law. Multiple separate laws do not aggregate for this question; any one law must meet or exceed the threshold on its own.

Inclusions and exclusions:
- Include rescission provisions enacted in any law (standalone rescissions act, appropriations/omnibus, or other statute) so long as the law’s text rescinds definite dollar amounts of budget authority.
- Exclude proposed rescissions (special messages) that are not enacted into law.
- Exclude rescissions with indefinite amounts (“up to,” “not more than,” “such sums as may be necessary”); include “not less than” at the stated minimum.
- Exclude administrative withholdings or deferrals absent enacted rescission; ICA requires funds proposed for rescission be made available if Congress does not act within the statutory period.

Resolution:
- Resolve Yes if there exists at least one Public Law enacted within the window whose text rescinds definite amounts of budget authority summing to ≥ $2,000,000,000.
- Resolve No otherwise.

Primary resolution source and method:
- Use Congress.gov to identify laws enacted in the window and to access their text and Public Law status. Example format/reference: the Public Law page for H.R.4, which shows Public Law number and enactment date.
- Compute the total by summing the definite rescinded amounts in the enacted law’s text, applying GAO’s definiteness rules.

Secondary/confirmatory sources (if needed):
- White House/O.M.B. materials (special messages) to understand targeted accounts and amounts proposed, noting that only enacted text governs.
- GAO ICA explainer and 2 U.S.C. § 683 for process context and timeline constraints.

Edge cases:
- If a law rescinds amounts both definite and indefinite, count only the definite amounts.
- If a law states multiple rescissions across accounts, all definite rescinded amounts within that law are summed.
- If a veto override enacts a law on Dec 31, use the official enactment date/time in UTC as displayed on Congress.gov; enactment outside the window does not count even if effective date falls inside the window.

question: Will the Federal Reserve lower the federal funds rate target range midpoint by at least 100 basis points by 2025-12-31 (UTC), relative to 2025-09-15?
background: Context for forecasters: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets a target range for the federal funds rate, the interest rate at which depository institutions lend balances to each other overnight. Cuts in the policy rate are typically implemented in 25 basis point increments. Policy rates influence broader financing conditions, including commercial borrowing costs. This question operationalizes “a 100 bp cut” as a change in the midpoint of the FOMC’s target range of at least 1.00 percentage point between a fixed baseline date and the end date. Definitions: federal funds rate (see: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_funds_rate), basis point (see: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_point). Data used for resolution will come from the Federal Reserve Board’s monetary policy press releases and the St. Louis Fed’s FRED series for the Federal Funds Target Range Upper (DFEDTARU) and Lower (DFEDTARL). Forecasters should check those sources for the baseline (2025-09-15) and end-date (2025-12-31) values when forming priors.
resolution_criteria:
Start and end of measurement window: Baseline is the federal funds target range in effect at 2025-09-15 23:59:59 UTC. The end observation is the federal funds target range in effect at 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. The question resolves on the first business day after 2025-12-31 once sources are checked.

Quantity measured: Midpoint of the federal funds target range on each date, defined as (upper limit + lower limit)/2, in percentage points. If the FOMC targets a single point (no range) on either date, treat the upper and lower as equal to that point target.

Resolution rule: Resolve YES if the end-date midpoint is less than or equal to (baseline midpoint − 1.00). Otherwise resolve NO.

Primary sources (authoritative and recurring):
- Federal Reserve Board monetary policy press releases (FOMC statements): https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy.htm
- St. Louis Fed FRED series for Federal Funds Target Range – Upper Limit (DFEDTARU): https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU and Lower Limit (DFEDTARL): https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARL

Measurement procedure:
1) Determine the upper and lower limits in effect at the two specified timestamps using the Fed press releases or the FRED DFEDTARU/DFEDTARL daily values for those calendar dates. If both are available and disagree, prefer the Federal Reserve Board press release text for the decision that set the range in effect at the timestamp.
2) Compute the midpoint for each date as (upper+lower)/2.
3) Compute change = baseline midpoint − end-date midpoint.
4) If change ≥ 1.00 percentage points (100 bps), resolve YES; else NO.

Edge cases and tie-breaking:
- If the policy target changes intraday on 2025-12-31, use the range in effect at 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-12-31.
- If sources are temporarily unavailable on the resolution date, use reputable wire services (e.g., Associated Press, Reuters, Bloomberg) or major newspapers (e.g., WSJ, NYT) reporting the announced target range; verify against archived copies when available.
- No rounding beyond the precision published by the Fed/FRED is applied; midpoints are calculated using the exact published upper and lower values.

question: Will OPEC+’s official required-production sum for its eight participating countries be ≥250,000 bpd higher in December 2025 than in September 2025?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- What is OPEC+? OPEC+ refers to the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries together with other cooperating oil‑producing countries, formed in late 2016 to coordinate production policy. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OPEC
- How OPEC+ states targets: In 2025 communications, OPEC press releases for a subgroup of eight participating countries have used the term “required production level” and announced month‑to‑month “production adjustments” relative to those required levels. The eight participating countries are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, and Oman. OPEC has noted these adjustments can be paused or reversed depending on market conditions. Example PR (May 3, 2025): https://www.opec.org/pr-detail/563-03-may-2025.html
- 2024 baseline and unwind: On June 2, 2024, OPEC+ extended deep production cuts into 2025, including extending 3.66 mb/d of cuts to end‑2025 and phasing out 2.2 mb/d of voluntary cuts from October 2024 to September 2025, with the option to pause or reverse the unwind. Capacity target talks were pushed to November 2025.
- Developments in 2025: OPEC+ agreed to raise output by 137,000 bpd in October 2025, decided by eight members in an online meeting, while noting it could accelerate, pause, or reverse future hikes. Reuters reported earlier monthly boosts in mid‑2025 were larger (e.g., 411,000 bpd in June/July; 555,000 bpd in August/September), and that the October step represented a slowdown. The group also indicated it had begun unwinding a second tranche of cuts ahead of schedule. Reuters subsequently reported OPEC+ was likely to approve another production increase of at least 137,000 bpd for November 2025, to be decided at an October 5 meeting; that article did not mention December plans.
- Market outlook: The U.S. EIA stated on 2025-08-12 that OPEC+ announced it would unwind its cuts by September 2025 (a year ahead of the prior schedule), and the EIA expected supply to outpace demand, inventories to grow, and Brent to average below $60/bbl in Q4 2025.
- Where targets are published: OPEC’s Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR) is a monthly analytical publication and is typically not the channel for announcing formal OPEC+ production targets; formal targets and “required production levels” for the eight‑country subgroup have appeared in OPEC press releases/communiqués. See MOMR: https://www.opec.org/monthly-oil-market-report.html
- Units: One oil barrel (bbl) equals exactly 42 U.S. gallons (approximately 159 liters). “bpd” denotes barrels per day. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrel_(unit)
Why this is non‑trivial: As of late September 2025, an October +137 kbpd increase has been agreed and at least another +137 kbpd for November is anticipated, but OPEC+ retains flexibility to pause or reverse increases, leaving the net change between September and December 2025 uncertain. The EIA’s outlook suggests additional pressure to increase supply into late 2025, yet price dynamics might prompt caution.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome to resolve between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
Definition of key terms and scope:
- OPEC+ means OPEC members plus cooperating non‑OPEC producers, as described here: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OPEC.
- Eight participating countries refers to the subgroup explicitly listed by OPEC in 2025 production‑adjustment press releases: Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, UAE, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, and Oman.
- Required production level is the official per‑country target level used in OPEC’s 2025 press releases when announcing month‑to‑month production adjustments for the eight participating countries (e.g., “a production adjustment of 411 thousand barrels per day in June 2025 from May 2025 required production level”). This terminology and approach are documented in OPEC’s May 3, 2025 press release.
- Barrel and bpd: One barrel (bbl) equals exactly 42 U.S. gallons; bpd = barrels per day. Calculations are done in bpd (not thousand bpd).
What is measured:
- Let S_sep be the sum of the required production levels (in bpd) for the eight participating countries applicable to September 2025.
- Let S_dec be the sum of the required production levels (in bpd) for the same eight countries applicable to December 2025.
Resolution rule:
- YES if S_dec − S_sep ≥ 250,000 bpd. NO otherwise.
Source hierarchy and how to determine S_sep and S_dec:
1) Primary sources: OPEC/OPEC+ official communications (press releases, meeting communiqués) that specify per‑country required production levels and/or month‑specific targets for the eight participating countries. Example of the relevant format and terminology: OPEC PR, May 3, 2025. OPEC official publications are hosted on https://www.opec.org/ (Press Releases section).
2) If a primary source specifying the exact per‑country required production levels for September 2025 and/or December 2025 is not publicly available by 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC, rely on reputable wire‑service reports that directly and unambiguously quote OPEC/OPEC+ official target figures or month‑on‑month adjustments from those official communications. Acceptable outlets include Reuters (Energy/OPEC section: https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/opec/), Bloomberg, or the Associated Press. For context on recent reporting style and substance, see: Reuters on October +137 kbpd  and on expected November +≥137 kbpd.
3) If multiple sources conflict, precedence is: OPEC communication(s) > Reuters > Bloomberg > Associated Press. Use the latest applicable document available by the resolution timestamp.
How to compute and handle units/rounding:
- Use the per‑country required production figures as stated. If a figure is provided in thousand bpd, convert to bpd by multiplying by 1,000. Sum the eight countries’ figures to obtain S_sep and S_dec. Compute S_dec − S_sep to the nearest barrel (no additional rounding beyond the source precision).
- Only targets/required production levels count; actual realized production does not affect resolution.
Temporal and eligibility notes:
- The question compares targets applicable to September 2025 and December 2025. For S_sep, use the last official required production levels applicable to September 2025 as of 2025‑09‑30 23:59:59 UTC. For S_dec, use the last official required production levels applicable to December 2025 available by 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC.
- Forecasting period: 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC through 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC. This window defines when the market participant is forecasting the outcome; it does not restrict use of earlier documents needed to establish September 2025 targets.
- If OPEC+ announces ranges rather than point targets for required production levels, use the clearly identified “required production level” point figure. If only a range exists and no point figure is identified by 2025‑12‑31, resolve using the lower bound of the range to define each country’s required production level for summation.
Why this is resolvable:
- OPEC’s 2025 press releases for the eight‑country subgroup explicitly reference “required production levels” and month‑to‑month adjustments, and note that increases can be paused or reversed. Reuters’ reporting documents both agreed and anticipated month‑specific increases and the eight‑member decision mechanism. The EIA documents the broader unwind timeline into September 2025. OPEC’s MOMR is monthly analysis (not the venue for the targets themselves). Together, these sources provide clear, authoritative, and timely documentation to establish S_sep and S_dec and compute the difference by the resolution deadline.

question: Will the U.S. unemployment rate (U-3, seasonally adjusted) for November 2025 be 4.5% or higher when the BLS publishes the Employment Situation on December 5, 2025?
background:
Overview and status quo as of September 30, 2025
- What is being forecast: The seasonally adjusted U.S. unemployment rate (U-3) for the reference month November 2025, as reported in the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Employment Situation news release scheduled for Friday, December 5, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time (ET).
- Definitions (authoritative BLS sources):
  • U-3 (official unemployment rate): Total unemployed as a percent of the civilian labor force; calculated as (unemployed ÷ labor force) × 100.
  • Unemployed (CPS): People with no employment during the survey reference week, who were available for work (except for temporary illness), and who made specific efforts to find employment during the 4‑week period ending with the reference week.
  • Labor force: All people age 16+ classified as either employed or unemployed.
  • Seasonally adjusted: Statistical procedure removing normal seasonal effects (e.g., holidays, school schedules, weather) to better reveal underlying trends.
- Current status: The latest published headline unemployment rate (seasonally adjusted U-3) was 4.3 percent for August 2025, and the release noted the rate "changed little" in August. The next Employment Situation report (covering September 2025) is scheduled for Friday, October 3, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. ET.
- Where to find the data at resolution time: BLS Employment Situation release page (the canonical landing page for the monthly report): https://www.bls.gov/news.release/empsit.htm. BLS’s release calendar confirms the Employment Situation for November 2025 is set for Friday, December 5, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. ET.
Why this question is non-trivial: The threshold (≥ 4.5%) is close to the recent reported level (4.3% for August 2025), making both “Yes” and “No” plausible depending on labor-market developments through November.
resolution_criteria:
How the question resolves
- Resolution window: This question resolves on the basis of the BLS Employment Situation news release published on Friday, December 5, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. ET, which covers the reference month November 2025.
- Exact test: "Yes" if the headline seasonally adjusted unemployment rate (U-3) for November 2025, as published in the BLS Employment Situation news release on that date, is greater than or equal to 4.5%. Otherwise, "No".
- What value to use: Use the seasonally adjusted U-3 unemployment rate for the United States, as presented in the December 5, 2025 Employment Situation news release (e.g., in the summary and accompanying tables). Do not use any later revisions, benchmarking updates, or corrections published after the initial release; resolution is based on the first official publication on December 5, 2025.
- Scope and definitions (for clarity):
  • "U-3" means the official unemployment rate: total unemployed as a percent of the civilian labor force.
  • "Unemployed," "labor force," and "seasonally adjusted" are defined per BLS Current Population Survey concepts.
  • "Reported by BLS" means posted on the BLS Employment Situation news release page: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/empsit.htm.
- Contingencies: If BLS reschedules the December 5, 2025 release, resolve using the first official Employment Situation news release that includes November 2025 data (i.e., the earliest publication that reports the November 2025 U-3). If multiple versions are posted the same day (e.g., corrected PDFs), use the earliest official publication time-stamped by BLS.
- Primary resolution sources:
  • BLS Employment Situation release page: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/empsit.htm.
  • BLS release calendar confirming date/time: https://www.bls.gov/schedule/news_release/current_year.asp (entry: Employment Situation for November 2025 — Friday, December 5, 2025, 08:30 AM ET).

question: Will U.S. headline CPI-U (12-month change) for October 2025 be ≥ 3.0%?
background:
Context and current status (as of 2025-09-30):
- What is being measured: The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI‑U) measures the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of goods and services; the “all items” index refers to the overall CPI for all urban consumers. The “12‑month percent change” compares the index level for a given month to the same month one year earlier and, in the CPI news release, is reported “before seasonal adjustment” (i.e., not seasonally adjusted).
- Latest published reading: In the most recent national CPI news release available as of this writing (covering August 2025), “Over the last 12 months, the all items index increased 2.9 percent before seasonal adjustment.” The release also notes: “The Consumer Price Index for September 2025 is scheduled to be released on Wednesday, October 15, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. (ET).” 
- How BLS presents the number: The CPI news release tabulates the 12‑month change for “All items” in Table 1, shown to one decimal place under the “Unadjusted percent change” columns.
- Relevant upcoming methodology note: With the release of October 2025 data on November 13, 2025, BLS will remove long-term care (LTC) insurance from the health insurance index used within the CPI medical care category, due to market changes rendering LTC out of scope for the CPI market basket.
- Release timing for the target month: The BLS schedule lists “Consumer Price Index for October 2025” for Thursday, November 13, 2025 at 08:30 AM (Eastern Time).

Why this is forecastable: As of August 2025, headline YoY CPI‑U was 2.9%. Whether October’s YoY prints at or above 3.0% depends on movements in components such as energy and shelter, base effects from October 2024, and any small measurement changes, leaving reasonable uncertainty through the November 13, 2025 release.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve “Yes” if the 12‑month percent change in the U.S. CPI‑U “All items” index for October 2025 is greater than or equal to 3.0% as published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) in its CPI news release for October 2025 on November 13, 2025; otherwise resolve “No”.

Authoritative source and where to read the number:
- Primary source: BLS “Consumer Price Index Summary” news release web page for the October 2025 data published on November 13, 2025, 08:30 AM Eastern Time (ET). Use the value appearing in Table 1 (“Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI‑U): U.S. city average, by expenditure category”), in the “Unadjusted percent change” 12‑month column for “All items,” which is reported to one decimal place. The scheduled publication date/time is listed on the BLS release calendar as Thursday, November 13, 2025 at 08:30 AM (ET).

Definitions and clarifications:
- CPI‑U “All items” refers to the overall Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (U.S. city average) produced by BLS.
- “12‑month percent change” is the percent change from October 2024 to October 2025 in the not seasonally adjusted CPI‑U all‑items index; BLS describes the headline 12‑month change in the news release as “before seasonal adjustment”.
- Rounding/tie rule: Use the value as published to one decimal place in the CPI news release Table 1. A published value of 3.0% counts as meeting the ≥ 3.0% threshold (i.e., “Yes”). If the value in the news release narrative text and Table 1 differ (rare), Table 1 governs.
- Scope note: BLS indicates that with the release of October 2025 data, long‑term care (LTC) insurance is removed from the CPI health insurance index; this is informational background only and does not change the resolution approach.

Timing and contingencies:
- Resolution will occur after the October 2025 CPI news release is published on November 13, 2025 at 08:30 AM ET, which falls within the overall October 15–December 31, 2025 resolution window.
- If BLS issues an official correction (erratum) to the October 2025 CPI news release by December 31, 2025 that changes the Table 1 12‑month value for “All items,” the corrected value will be used; otherwise, the initially published value on November 13, 2025 will govern.
- If, contrary to schedule, BLS does not publish the October 2025 CPI news release by December 31, 2025, resolve as N/A.

question: Will the Reserve Bank of India change the policy repo rate at its December 3–5, 2025 Monetary Policy Committee meeting?
background:
Summary of what forecasters need to know as of 2025-09-30 (IST)

- What is being decided and by whom: The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is the body responsible for setting India’s benchmark policy interest rate. The MPC meets at least once per quarter and publishes its decision after each meeting.

- What is the “policy repo rate”: In India’s Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), the policy repo rate is the interest rate at which the RBI lends to banks via repurchase agreements; it is the key policy rate used by the MPC to signal the monetary stance.

- When the relevant meeting is scheduled: According to widely reported coverage of the RBI’s FY 2025–26 MPC calendar, the December 2025 MPC meeting is scheduled for December 3, 4, and 5, 2025 (IST).

- Where the decision will be published: The RBI publishes its Monetary Policy Statements and “Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)” as official press releases on its Press Releases portal. Past MPC resolutions appear there on the last day of the meeting, indicating this is the canonical source to check for the repo rate decision.

- Status quo (current level): As of late September 2025, the policy repo rate stands at 5.50%, and a Reuters poll at that time expected the RBI to hold at 5.50% at the Sep 29–Oct 1 meeting as well.

Key terms and references
- Monetary Policy Committee (India): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_Policy_Committee_(India) 
- Liquidity Adjustment Facility (definition underpinning the repo rate): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquidity_adjustment_facility 
- RBI Press Releases portal (source of the MPC resolution and policy statement): https://www.rbi.org.in/commonman/English/scripts/pressreleases.aspx 
- December 2025 MPC meeting dates reported: https://www.moneycontrol.com/banking/rbi-releases-mpc-meeting-schedule-for-fy26-here-are-the-dates-article-12976619.html 
- Current repo rate (late Sep 2025) and expectations: https://www.reuters.com/world/india/reuters-poll-reserve-bank-india-hold-repo-rate-550-october-1-said-45-61-2025-09-24/ 

All dates/times are India Standard Time (IST; UTC+05:30) unless noted otherwise.
resolution_criteria:
Operationalization and scope
- Time window: This market resolves based on the RBI’s December 2025 MPC decision announced between 00:00 IST on December 1, 2025 and 23:59 IST on December 31, 2025. All dates/times are IST (UTC+05:30).
- Focal event: The first RBI press release for the MPC meeting scheduled on December 3–5, 2025 (IST) that contains the “Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)” and/or the “Monetary Policy Statement” will be used to determine the outcome.

Definitions (to remove ambiguity)
- “Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)”: The RBI committee responsible for fixing the benchmark policy interest rate in India.
- “Policy repo rate”: The interest rate at which the RBI lends to banks under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility; it is the key policy rate in India.
- “Change” in the policy repo rate: Any increase or decrease in the policy repo rate level relative to the level in effect immediately prior to the December 2025 MPC announcement, as determined by comparing the rate stated in the December 2025 MPC resolution/statement with the rate level stated in the most recent prior MPC resolution/statement.

Resolution rule (Yes/No)
- Resolve Yes if the RBI’s official press release for the December 2025 MPC meeting explicitly states that the policy repo rate has been increased or decreased, or if it states a policy repo rate level that differs from the level in effect immediately prior (as per the last MPC resolution/statement).
- Resolve No if the press release explicitly states that the policy repo rate is unchanged, or if the level stated matches the level in effect immediately prior (as per the last MPC resolution/statement).

Source of truth and document precedence
- Primary source: RBI Press Releases portal page hosting the relevant press release(s) (the “Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)” and/or “Monetary Policy Statement”) for the December 2025 meeting. If both an HTML page and a linked PDF are available for the same press release, either may be used so long as it is RBI-hosted.
- Document precedence: If multiple documents are released for the same meeting, precedence is: (1) “Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)”, then (2) “Monetary Policy Statement”, then (3) any errata/corrigendum specific to that meeting released by RBI within 48 hours of the initial release. If RBI issues a correction within 48 hours, the corrected version governs.

Scheduling contingencies (to ensure resolvability)
- Rescheduling within December 2025: If the December 3–5, 2025 MPC meeting is officially rescheduled but still occurs within December 2025 (IST), the first RBI press release carrying the MPC resolution/statement for that rescheduled December meeting will be used for resolution.
- Postponement beyond December 31, 2025 or cancellation: If no MPC resolution/statement corresponding to the December 2025 meeting is published by 23:59 IST on December 31, 2025 (because the meeting is postponed beyond that date or cancelled), resolve No.

Practical notes
- Typical publication timing: Historically, MPC resolutions are posted on the RBI Press Releases portal on the last day of the meeting, which for a Dec 3–5, 2025 schedule would typically be Dec 5, 2025 (IST). Forecasters should check the portal on and after that date.

Context as of today for forecasters
- Meeting dates: December 3–5, 2025 (IST) per reporting on the RBI FY 2025–26 MPC calendar.
- Current policy repo rate: 5.50% as of late September 2025, with a contemporaneous poll expecting a hold at that level at the Sep 29–Oct 1 meeting.

Verification time budget
- A resolver should be able to verify the outcome within 10 minutes by locating the December 2025 MPC resolution/statement on the RBI Press Releases portal and reading whether the policy repo rate was changed or left unchanged.

question: Between 2025-09-22 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will the FOMC’s federal funds rate target range upper bound be at least 50 basis points lower on 2025-12-31 than on 2025-09-22?
background:
Definitions and context a forecaster needs:
- Federal funds rate: The interest rate at which depository institutions lend balances to each other overnight; since 2008 the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets a target range with a lower and upper bound. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_funds_rate
- FOMC: The body within the Federal Reserve System that sets monetary policy, including the target range for the federal funds rate. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Open_Market_Committee
- Target range (upper bound): The upper limit of the FOMC’s target range for the federal funds rate. Example: a range stated as “4 to 4-1/4 percent” has an upper bound of 4.25%.
- Basis point (bp): One hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%), i.e., 0.0001 in decimal. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_point
Status quo as of today (2025-09-22): On 2025-09-17, the FOMC lowered the target range by 0.25 percentage points to 4.00%–4.25%, effective 2025-09-18. The Federal Reserve’s implementation note explicitly states “maintain the federal funds rate in a target range of 4 to 4-1/4 percent” effective 2025-09-18. The St. Louis Fed FRED “Federal Funds Target Range – Upper Limit (DFEDTARU)” series shows the upper bound moved from 4.50% on 2025-09-17 to 4.25% on 2025-09-18, remaining 4.25% through 2025-09-19–21.
Why this matters: Measuring net change in the upper bound provides an unambiguous proxy for cumulative rate cuts, avoids ambiguity around intra-range changes or midpoint conventions, and has high-quality public data available for resolution.
resolution_criteria:
Start and end window:
- Eligible period: 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
Primary measure and source:
- Measure the upper bound of the FOMC’s federal funds rate target range on the start date and on the end date, using the St. Louis Fed FRED series “Federal Funds Target Range – Upper Limit (DFEDTARU)”: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU.
- If FRED is unavailable or shows a gap for the specific dates needed, use the Federal Reserve Board’s post-meeting press releases and Implementation Notes to identify the target range in effect on those dates: https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases.htm (specifically, the 2025-09-17 statement and implementation note establish the current range).
Resolution rule:
- YES if: Upper bound on 2025-12-31 (as represented by DFEDTARU for that date in UTC) is at least 50 basis points (0.50 percentage points) lower than the upper bound on 2025-09-22.
- NO otherwise.
Clarifications:
- “Upper bound” means the upper limit of the target range. If, at any point, the FOMC sets a single-point target instead of a range, treat that single point as the upper bound for this question.
- Ignore the effective federal funds rate (EFFR); only the target range as set by the FOMC is relevant.
- If multiple changes occur on 2025-12-31, the range in effect at 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC governs.
- If the start date’s range changes on 2025-09-22, use the value in effect at 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC (as represented by DFEDTARU’s value for 2025-09-22).

question: Will Archer’s “Midnight” (Model M001) receive an FAA Type Certificate by December 31, 2025?
background:
Summary of what forecasters need to know as of 2025-09-30:
- Aircraft and program: “Midnight” is Archer Aviation Inc.’s electric powered‑lift air taxi. In FAA documents it is designated the Archer Aviation, Inc. Model M001 powered‑lift, a special‑class aircraft intended for Parts 91 and 135 operations; the FAA finalized special‑class airworthiness criteria for this model on 2024‑05‑24. The criteria describe its configuration (12 electric motors/props; tilt on six forward props; pilot + four passengers) and the special‑class certification path under 14 CFR 21.17(b).
- What a Type Certificate (TC) is: Under 14 CFR §21.41, a TC includes the type design, operating limitations, the Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS), applicable regulations with which the FAA records compliance, and any other prescribed conditions/limitations. For resolution, the TC is evidenced by publication of a TCDS in the FAA’s Dynamic Regulatory System (DRS) or an official FAA issuance notice.
- Powered‑lift definition: The FAA defines powered‑lift aircraft as capable of vertical takeoff, vertical landing, and low‑speed flight; many are electric VTOL “air taxis”. Midnight falls in this powered‑lift category per the FAA’s criteria.
- How/where TCs are listed: The FAA states that TCDS documents can be located via the FAA website/DRS; this is the canonical place to find an aircraft’s TCDS and confirm issuance.
- Program status and milestones in 2024–2025: Archer secured key operational/maintenance certificates on the path to commercialization: Part 145 repair station certification (2024‑02‑08) ; Part 135 air carrier & operator certificate (2024‑06‑05) ; and Part 141 flight school certification for its pilot training academy (2025‑02‑18). On 2025‑09‑22, Archer reported a Midnight flight‑test milestone reaching 7,000 ft, with a 45‑mile flight at >120 mph as part of envelope expansion; a prior flight covered ~55 miles in 31 minutes at >126 mph. These releases underscore progress but (as of their dates) do not announce TC issuance.

Why this question is plausibly uncertain: The FAA has finalized airworthiness criteria for the model and Archer has progressed on Part 135/141/145 and flight testing, but initial eVTOL type certifications are novel and complex; timing by year‑end 2025 remains genuinely uncertain yet objectively verifiable via FAA records.
resolution_criteria:
This market resolves based on whether the FAA has issued a Type Certificate (TC) for Archer Aviation Inc.’s Model M001 powered‑lift (commonly branded “Midnight”) between 2025‑01‑01 00:00:00 UTC and 2026‑01‑01 04:59:59 UTC (which corresponds to 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 Eastern Time, UTC‑5).

Definitions and sources:
- Type Certificate (TC): As defined in 14 CFR §21.41, a TC includes the type design, operating limitations, the Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS), the applicable regulations with which the FAA records compliance, and any other prescribed conditions or limitations.
- Relevant product: Archer Aviation Inc. Model M001 powered‑lift (the FAA’s designation for Archer’s “Midnight”), certified as a special‑class powered‑lift per the FAA’s published criteria. Powered‑lift aircraft are defined by the FAA as capable of vertical takeoff/landing and low‑speed flight.
- Primary resolution source: FAA Dynamic Regulatory System (DRS) listing of a TCDS for Archer Aviation Inc. Model M001 powered‑lift (e.g., the presence of a TCDS entry for Model M001 in DRS). The FAA’s guidance indicates TCDS are available via the FAA website/DRS.

Resolution rules:
- Resolve Yes if, by the deadline above, any of the following are true:
  1) The FAA DRS contains a Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS) for Archer Aviation Inc. Model M001 powered‑lift, indicating the TC has been issued; or
  2) The FAA publishes an official announcement or database entry clearly stating that a Type Certificate has been issued for Archer Aviation Inc. Model M001 powered‑lift (e.g., an FAA press/news release or official FAA database record of a TC issuance for Model M001).
- Resolve No if neither condition is met by the deadline.
- Evidence and tie‑breakers: The resolver should first search the FAA DRS for a TCDS for “Archer Aviation Inc.” and “Model M001” (or equivalent TC numbering). If DRS is unavailable at the time of resolution, the resolver may use an official FAA announcement as specified above. Company press releases or third‑party media may be considered corroborating but are insufficient on their own unless they link to or are explicitly mirrored by official FAA publications.
- Time zone: All times are interpreted as stated above; the cutoff is 2026‑01‑01 04:59:59 UTC (2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 Eastern Time, UTC‑5).

Notes for resolvers:
- The FAA finalized special‑class airworthiness criteria for the Archer Aviation Inc. Model M001 powered‑lift on 2024‑05‑24. This is background only; issuance of airworthiness criteria is not itself a Type Certificate issuance under §21.41.
- As of the latest cited Archer and FAA materials in 2024–2025, Archer has received Part 145 (2024‑02‑08), Part 135 (2024‑06‑05), and Part 141 (2025‑02‑18), and has continued flight‑test expansion through September 2025. These do not constitute a TC. The question resolves solely on TC issuance as defined above.

question: Between 00:00 UTC Oct 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC Dec 31, 2025, will an official U.S. government website publish an announcement of at least $100 million USD in new humanitarian assistance for Palestinian civilians in Gaza?
background:
Context and recent precedent
- The U.S. government has periodically announced large, discrete packages of humanitarian assistance for Palestinians, often via official press releases or statements. For example, on October 18, 2023, the White House announced $100 million in humanitarian assistance for Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank. In June 2024, the United States announced an additional $404 million in life‑saving humanitarian aid to support Palestinian civilians in Gaza, the West Bank, and the region.
- In early 2025, U.S. foreign assistance underwent a significant procedural change: on January 24, 2025, the Secretary of State ordered a pause in all new obligations of foreign assistance pending an 85‑day review; a narrow waiver for “emergency food assistance” was initially granted and subsequently expanded on January 28, 2025 to include disbursements under existing “lifesaving humanitarian assistance” programs. USAID OIG reported that these actions affected the ability to disburse and oversee humanitarian programming, including in high‑risk environments like Gaza.
- Humanitarian assistance (also termed humanitarian aid) refers to immediate, short‑term material and logistical support to save lives, alleviate suffering, and maintain human dignity, distinct from longer‑term development aid.

What forecasters should watch
- Official U.S. government communications channels that have historically carried such announcements, including: White House Briefing Room (https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/), U.S. Department of State Press Releases/Media Notes (https://www.state.gov/press-releases/; https://www.state.gov/media-notes/), and USAID Press Releases (https://www.usaid.gov/news-information/press-releases). Past announcements cited above illustrate the format and language typically used (“announces additional humanitarian assistance,” “new aid”).
- Policy and operational constraints in 2025 (e.g., the January 2025 pause and limited waivers) that could affect the likelihood, timing, or scale of any new announcements.

Definitions and geographic scope (for context)
- Gaza/Gaza Strip: the Palestinian territory on the Mediterranean bordered by Israel and Egypt; references to “Gaza” in U.S. announcements typically denote this territory as the beneficiary area.
- Palestinian people: an Arab ethnonational group native to Palestine; U.S. announcements often refer to “Palestinian civilians” when designating beneficiaries.

Status as of 2025‑10‑01
- As of the question’s publication date, forecasters should use the 2023–2024 precedents for scale and phrasing of announcements and the 2025 policy context to inform their estimates.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and time zone
- The eligible window runs from 00:00 UTC on 2025‑10‑15 through 23:59 UTC on 2025‑12‑31, inclusive. If an official page displays only a calendar date (no time), that date must fall within this window to qualify.

What resolves “Yes”
- A “Yes” resolution requires at least one qualifying announcement, posted within the window, on an official U.S. government executive branch website (a.gov domain controlled by the White House or an executive department/agency such as whitehouse.gov, state.gov, or usaid.gov), that:
  1) Publicly announces a single package of humanitarian assistance (aka humanitarian aid) ; and
  2) Explicitly identifies Palestinian civilians in Gaza as beneficiaries (Gaza alone or Gaza together with the West Bank and/or the region); and
  3) States a total amount for that package of at least $100,000,000 (one hundred million U.S. dollars). The amount must be unambiguous and represent a firm commitment (e.g., “announces $X,” “will provide $X,” “additional $X”). Language such as “up to $X” does not qualify unless a minimum equal to or greater than $100,000,000 is also explicitly stated; and
  4) Characterizes the funding as new or additional relative to prior U.S. commitments (e.g., uses words like “new,” “additional,” or equivalent), indicating that this is not merely a restatement of cumulative totals.

Definitions and counting rules
- Humanitarian assistance/humanitarian aid: immediate, short‑term material/logistics aid to save lives and alleviate suffering; excludes military/security assistance and development/reconstruction funding unless the announcement itself characterizes it as humanitarian assistance/aid.
- Gaza/Gaza Strip: the territory commonly referred to as Gaza; references to “Gaza” in the announcement satisfy the geographic condition. “Palestinian civilians” refers to members of the Palestinian people as commonly understood in humanitarian contexts.
- Package: a discrete funding commitment announced in a single official communication. If a qualifying announcement lists multiple line items for Palestinians (e.g., food, medical, shelter) within the same communication, those amounts may be summed to determine whether the $100,000,000 threshold is met. If an announcement covers multiple countries/beneficiaries, only the amounts explicitly designated for Palestinians (with Gaza included) may be counted toward the threshold.
- Currency: The qualifying announcement must state the package amount in U.S. dollars (USD). If multiple currencies are shown, a USD figure must be present in the same announcement.

Exclusions (do not count)
- Media reporting or third‑party summaries without a corresponding official U.S. government executive branch web page meeting the criteria.
- Announcements that solely restate cumulative totals provided “since [year]” without a distinct new/additional package meeting the threshold.
- Announcements that use only “up to $X” without stating a committed minimum ≥ $100,000,000.
- Military/security assistance or non‑humanitarian development/reconstruction funding unless the announcement explicitly frames it as humanitarian assistance/aid.
