question: Will Meta or Adam Mosseri publicly state that Threads has at least 500 million monthly active users between October 15 and December 31, 2025?
background:
Overview and current status as of 2025-09-30:
- Product in question: Threads is Meta’s text-based social network. For term clarity, see the Threads (social network) page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threads_(social_network).
- Recent official user numbers: On 2025-08-12, Adam Mosseri (Head of Instagram) publicly stated that Threads has “more than 400 million monthly active users (MAUs).” TechCrunch reported the announcement and linked Mosseri’s post; the article also notes Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had said in late April that Threads topped 350M MAUs.
- Usage momentum: Third-party analytics (Similarweb) cited by TechCrunch show Threads recorded 115.1M daily active users (DAUs) on mobile (iOS/Android) in June 2025, up 127.8% YoY. In late September 2025, Forbes (citing Similarweb) reported Threads briefly surpassed X (formerly Twitter) in global mobile DAUs for the first time and included multiple daily comparisons from mid-to-late September. Forbes also reported a Zuckerberg remark that Instagram now has 3 billion monthly active users.
- Why this is non-trivial: The event requires both reaching the threshold and a qualifying public disclosure by a specific set of official speakers/channels within the stated window. Meta does not routinely publish MAUs for Threads on a fixed schedule, so whether they will state ≥500M MAUs before year-end is uncertain despite strong growth indicators.

Key terms and definitions for this question:
- “Threads”: Meta’s social networking product branded “Threads.” It must be unambiguously the Threads service (not Instagram, Facebook, or WhatsApp). Reference link for context: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threads_(social_network).
- “Monthly active users” (“MAUs”): For resolution purposes here, this means the metric explicitly named “monthly active users,” “MAUs,” or “monthly active people” by Meta or the speaker in the qualifying statement. Statements about “daily active users” (DAUs), “weekly active users,” “registered users/accounts,” “downloads,” “web visits,” or similar do not count.
- “Publicly state”: A statement that is published to the general public (not a private communication) via one of the qualifying official channels listed below.
- “Qualifying official channels”: Any of the following:
  1) Meta or Instagram official websites/blogs/newsrooms (e.g., https://about.fb.com/news/),
  2) Meta SEC filings (e.g., on EDGAR: https://www.sec.gov/edgar/search/#/category/company),
  3) Direct public posts by Mark Zuckerberg or Adam Mosseri on their official social profiles on Threads, Instagram, or Facebook.
- “Qualifying phrasing”: The statement must explicitly assert that Threads has at least 500,000,000 monthly active users. Acceptable phrasings include “≥500 million MAUs,” “at least 500 million monthly active users,” “over 500 million monthly active users,” etc., provided it clearly refers to Threads.
- Language: Statements in any language are acceptable if they meet the criteria above; translations are acceptable if the original post is accessible and the numeric threshold is unambiguous.

Status quo data points (for context, not for resolution):
- 400M MAUs announcement by Mosseri on 2025-08-12.
- 115.1M mobile DAUs in June 2025 per Similarweb (as cited by TechCrunch).
- Threads surpassing X in mobile DAUs at several points in mid-to-late September 2025 (as cited by Forbes/Similarweb).

Notes on what will NOT count:
- Any third-party estimate without an official Meta/Zuckerberg/Mosseri statement does not count.
- Statements that do not mention “monthly” (e.g., only “users,” “DAUs,” “web visits”) do not count.
- Combined or aggregated metrics that include services other than Threads (e.g., “Instagram+Threads”) do not count.
- Statements published outside the specified window do not count, even if reported during the window.
resolution_criteria:
This resolves to Yes if and only if all of the following are true:
- Time window: A qualifying statement is published between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2026-01-01 07:59:59 UTC (the latter is equivalent to 2025-12-31 23:59:59 Pacific Time).
- Speaker/channel: The statement appears on a qualifying official channel, defined above (Meta/Instagram official site/blog/newsroom; Meta SEC filing; direct public posts by Mark Zuckerberg or Adam Mosseri on their official Threads/Instagram/Facebook profiles).
- Content: The statement explicitly says that Threads has at least 500,000,000 monthly active users (MAUs), using unambiguous phrasing that clearly refers to Threads.

Acceptable resolution sources:
- A URL to the qualifying statement itself (e.g., a Meta/Instagram Newsroom post; a post on Zuckerberg’s or Mosseri’s official profile; an SEC filing on EDGAR).
- Reputable media coverage (e.g., TechCrunch, The Verge, Reuters, AP, Bloomberg) only if it directly quotes or embeds the qualifying statement and the original statement is publicly accessible via a link. Coverage may be used to aid verification but the original qualifying statement must exist and be publicly accessible.

Resolution process:
- YES: Verifier confirms a qualifying statement was published within the window that meets all criteria above.
- NO: If no qualifying statement meeting the criteria is found by 2026-01-01 07:59:59 UTC, resolve No.

Context references informing the background (not used for resolution unless they themselves contain a qualifying statement within the window): TechCrunch’s report of Mosseri’s 400M MAUs announcement and Similarweb’s June 2025 DAUs ; Forbes’ report of Threads briefly surpassing X in mobile DAUs and Zuckerberg’s Instagram 3B MAUs remark.

question: Will U.S. CPI‑U (All Items, U.S. city average) 12‑month percent change for November 2025 be at least 3.3%?
background:
Overview and status quo as of 2025‑10‑01
- What is being measured: The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI‑U) measures the average change over time in prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of goods and services and covers over 90% of the U.S. population; the broad “All items” CPI‑U (U.S. city average, 1982‑84=100) is the most comprehensive headline index. The “12‑month percent change” (a.k.a. year‑over‑year, YoY) compares the index level to its level 12 months earlier; in BLS CPI news releases, the headline 12‑month percent change for All items is reported on a not seasonally adjusted basis (often phrased as “over the last 12 months … before seasonal adjustment”).
- Latest readings: As of October 1, 2025, the most recent published headline All items CPI‑U 12‑month change is for August 2025 at 2.9% (not seasonally adjusted), as stated in the BLS CPI Summary and on the CPI home page (“rose 2.9 percent over the last 12 months, not seasonally adjusted”). The CPI for September 2025 is scheduled to be released on Wednesday, October 15, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. ET.
- Relevant upcoming release: The BLS “Schedule of Selected Releases” lists “Consumer Price Index for November 2025” on Wednesday, December 10, 2025, at 08:30 AM (Eastern Time). Note on that page clarifies all times are Eastern Time; 08:30 ET corresponds to 13:30 UTC on 2025‑12‑10.

What forecasters should know
- Index and scope: This question uses the U.S. headline CPI‑U All items, U.S. city average, 1982‑84=100, not seasonally adjusted—i.e., the standard “headline inflation” figure cited in the first paragraph of BLS CPI news releases.
- Data source and publication: The canonical source will be the BLS CPI Summary news release page for the relevant month (HTML) and/or its accompanying PDF, which explicitly states the All items 12‑month percent change in the lead paragraph and tables.
- Timing: The November 2025 CPI report is scheduled for 2025‑12‑10 at 08:30 ET (13:30 UTC) per the BLS 2025 release calendar.

Definitions (for unambiguous resolution)
- CPI‑U: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, covering the urban population (over 90% of U.S. population).
- All items index: The broad headline CPI‑U for the U.S. city average, 1982‑84=100.
- 12‑month percent change (YoY): The percentage change in the not seasonally adjusted index level relative to the same month one year earlier; in BLS releases, the headline statement is “over the last 12 months … before seasonal adjustment”.
- “At least 3.3%”: Greater than or equal to 3.3%. All dates/times are in UTC unless explicitly labeled otherwise.
- Observation window: This question concerns the November 2025 reference month CPI‑U All items 12‑month percent change as first published by BLS on 2025‑12‑10; the observation period for this question runs from 2025‑10‑01 00:00 UTC through 2025‑12‑31 23:59 UTC, but only the 2025‑12‑10 publication is material to resolution.
resolution_criteria:
Resolve YES if, in the initial Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI Summary news release for November 2025 (published on 2025‑12‑10 at 08:30 ET / 13:30 UTC per the BLS calendar ), the headline All items CPI‑U (U.S. city average) 12‑month percent change (not seasonally adjusted) is greater than or equal to 3.3%, as stated in the narrative lead paragraph (e.g., “over the last 12 months … before seasonal adjustment”) or in the corresponding headline table showing the All items 12‑month percent change. Resolve NO otherwise.

Primary resolution source
- BLS CPI Summary (HTML): https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm — use the value explicitly stated for the All items CPI‑U 12‑month percent change for November 2025 in the narrative paragraph. If there is any ambiguity in the narrative, use the All items (U.S. city average) 12‑month percent change reported in the main table on the same page or in the accompanying PDF for the same release.

Tie‑breakers and contingencies
- If the HTML and PDF differ, prefer the HTML CPI Summary page value as of the time of initial publication on 2025‑12‑10 (13:30 UTC). If BLS issues a same‑day correction on 2025‑12‑10, use the corrected value posted on the CPI Summary page that day. Later revisions after 2025‑12‑10 do not affect resolution.
- The scheduled date/time for the November 2025 CPI release is per the BLS Schedule of Selected Releases; if BLS reschedules within 2025, resolution will occur upon publication of the November 2025 CPI Summary within the question’s observation window.

Notes for context (non‑binding but informative)
- Latest status: As of 2025‑10‑01, the most recent headline All items CPI‑U 12‑month change is 2.9% for August 2025 (not seasonally adjusted).
- Definitions and scope for CPI‑U and “All items” come from BLS CPI FAQs.

question: Will 2025 world oil demand growth be below 1.0 mb/d according to the latest IEA Oil Market Report published by 31 Dec 2025 (UTC)?
background:
Context for forecasters: This question is about whether the International Energy Agency (IEA) will assess that 2025 world oil demand grew by less than 1.0 million barrels per day (mb/d) versus 2024 when measured on an annual-average basis, as reported in its Oil Market Report (OMR). The IEA publishes monthly OMRs that include “world/total oil demand” annual levels and often an explicit y/y growth figure for the calendar year. Forecasters should consult the most recent 2025 OMR issues to see the current full‑year estimate and the IEA’s discussion of drivers (e.g., transport fuel demand, petrochemicals, electric vehicles, macroeconomic conditions, policy impacts). Key references:
- IEA Oil Market Report (monthly landing page): https://www.iea.org/reports/oil-market-report
- IEA OMR Glossary (scope/method notes for “oil demand” and units): https://www.iea.org/articles/oil-market-report-glossary
- IEA Glossary (definitions for kb/d and mb/d): https://www.iea.org/glossary
Definitions to know:
- World/total oil demand (IEA OMR usage): The OMR tracks “total oil” demand (sometimes termed total liquids), expressed as average million barrels per day over a calendar year. See OMR Glossary for scope and methodology.
- Barrels per day (b/d), thousand barrels per day (kb/d), and million barrels per day (mb/d): Unit conventions used by the IEA. See the IEA Glossary.
As of today (2025‑09‑22), the outcome is uncertain and depends on year‑end assessments; the IEA’s monthly OMR updates can change during the year. Forecasters should use the latest public IEA OMR, plus other reputable sources (e.g., OPEC MOMR, EIA STEO, macro indicators), to form a view. This question will resolve strictly on the IEA OMR as specified below.
resolution_criteria:
What is measured:
- Growth equals the IEA’s 2025 annual-average world (total) oil demand minus the IEA’s 2024 annual-average world (total) oil demand, both as presented in the same IEA Oil Market Report (OMR) used for resolution.

Primary source and timing:
- Use the latest IEA OMR published on or before 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC. The IEA OMR landing page is: https://www.iea.org/reports/oil-market-report. Within that report, use the world/total oil demand annual figures for 2025 and 2024.

How to extract the value:
- If the OMR provides an explicit 2025 y/y growth number for world/total oil demand, use that value.
- If only annual levels are presented, compute growth as (2025 annual average) − (2024 annual average) using the figures from the same OMR issue.

Scope, units, and comparisons:
- “World/total oil demand” follows the IEA OMR’s scope (total liquids) and methodology as described in the OMR Glossary: https://www.iea.org/articles/oil-market-report-glossary.
- Units: Use mb/d (million barrels per day). If values are shown in kb/d, convert at 1,000 kb/d = 1.0 mb/d. Unit definitions: https://www.iea.org/glossary.
- Precision: Compare using the highest-precision figure published in that OMR (e.g., two decimal places in mb/d) without additional rounding by the resolver.

Outcome rule:
- YES if growth < 1.00 mb/d.
- NO if growth ≥ 1.00 mb/d.

Discrepancies and precedence:
- If numerical values in OMR narrative text and OMR tables differ, tables take precedence. If multiple tables exist, prefer the summary “world/total oil demand” table that lists annual levels (or growth) by year.
- If more than one OMR is published on or before 2025‑12‑31, use the latest one.

Fallback if the OMR page is temporarily inaccessible:
- Accept the figure as quoted by a major international wire service (e.g., Reuters, Associated Press, or AFP) that explicitly attributes the exact 2025 world oil demand growth figure to the IEA OMR published on or before 2025‑12‑31, with a working link or clear date reference. If multiple such reports conflict, prefer the one that directly cites the OMR table figure.

Finality and revisions:
- The resolution uses the specified OMR available by 2025‑12‑31 UTC. Any later revisions or subsequent OMRs in 2026 or beyond do not affect the outcome.

question: Will the U.S. headline (U-3) unemployment rate reported in the Employment Situation for November 2025 be at least 4.3%?
background:
Overview: This question asks whether the seasonally adjusted U.S. unemployment rate (the official “headline” U‑3 measure) for the reference month November 2025, as reported in the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Employment Situation news release, will be greater than or equal to 4.3%.

Current status (as of 2025-10-01): The most recent published Employment Situation summary indicates that in August 2025 the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate (U‑3) was 4.3%, with 7.4 million people unemployed; the release stated these measures “changed little in August” and “also changed little over the year”.

Release timing: The Employment Situation for November 2025 is scheduled to be released on Friday, December 5, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time, per the BLS release calendars; the December 2025 calendar explicitly lists “Employment Situation — November 2025” on Dec 5 at 08:30 AM ET, and notes that all times are Eastern Time.

Key definitions:
- Employment Situation news release: BLS’s monthly national labor market report (published in HTML and PDF), which includes the seasonally adjusted U‑3 unemployment rate in the opening summary paragraph.
- Unemployment rate (U‑3): The official measure defined by BLS as “Total unemployed, as a percent of the civilian labor force (official unemployment rate),” derived from the Current Population Survey (CPS) and reported on a seasonally adjusted basis in the headline summary.

Why this matters for forecasters: The unemployment rate is a leading indicator of labor market tightness and economic conditions, sensitive to recent job growth, participation changes, and macro shocks. As of late 2025, the rate has been around the low-4% range, making a 4.3% threshold plausibly balanced and uncertain given recent data.

Primary data source for resolution: BLS Employment Situation news release page (HTML summary) for November 2025 (same URL used for current-month summary); the BLS also publishes a PDF version of the release, but the HTML summary will serve as the single source of truth if any discrepancy arises.
resolution_criteria:
Binary resolution (Yes/No) based on the first publication of the BLS Employment Situation news release for November 2025.

Operational details:
- Measurement: Use the seasonally adjusted U.S. unemployment rate (U‑3: total unemployed as a percent of the civilian labor force) as stated in the opening summary of the BLS Employment Situation HTML release for November 2025.
- Threshold comparison: Resolve Yes if the reported rate is greater than or equal to 4.3 percent; resolve No if it is less than 4.3 percent. Use the percentage exactly as printed in the release (BLS reports U‑3 to one decimal place); do not apply independent rounding.
- Source of truth: The BLS Employment Situation HTML page for the current-month summary (empsit.nr0.htm). If the HTML and PDF differ, use the HTML summary; if the HTML is temporarily unavailable at release but the PDF is available, use the PDF until the HTML becomes accessible, then confirm the HTML value. The August 2025 release format and content exemplify the source page to be used.
- Timing: The release is scheduled for Friday, December 5, 2025, at 08:30 a.m. Eastern Time; resolution will occur after that publication and no later than December 31, 2025.
- Revisions: If BLS issues revisions later the same day, use the first-published rate on the release date for resolution. Subsequent revisions after the release day will not affect resolution.
- Contingency: If the November 2025 Employment Situation is delayed but published by December 31, 2025, resolve on the first-published rate. If, in the unlikely event, it is not published by December 31, 2025, the question will be adjudicated based on credible reporting of the BLS November 2025 unemployment rate by major wire services (e.g., AP, Reuters) referencing the BLS figure; however, the primary expectation is timely publication per the BLS schedule.

question: Between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025 (UTC), will the United States or Colombia formally impose or initiate a new economic sanction or tariff measure specifically targeting the other country?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-09-30: U.S.–Colombia relations experienced multiple flashpoints in 2025. In January, the U.S. threatened across-the-board tariffs and other penalties over a dispute about deportation flights, but the two governments reached an agreement and Washington did not impose the threatened penalties. On July 3, 2025, the U.S. recalled its top diplomat from Bogotá; Colombia reciprocally recalled its ambassador to Washington the same day. On September 26–27, 2025, the U.S. State Department said it would revoke Colombian President Gustavo Petro’s U.S. visa following remarks at a New York protest; Petro criticized the move, alleging a violation of international law. The January tariff threats were withdrawn after the deportation-flights deal, and subsequent tensions reported to date have consisted of diplomatic recalls and the visa revocation episode rather than the imposition of new bilateral tariffs or economic sanctions.

Context on economic ties: The United States–Colombia Trade Promotion Agreement (CTPA) entered into force in 2012, liberalizing trade and eliminating many tariffs between the two countries. Any new tariff or sanction measure specifically targeting the other country would represent a material deterioration from the baseline of 2025-09-30.

Key definitions to use when interpreting the question:
- Economic sanctions: Commercial and financial penalties imposed by governments on other states, groups, or individuals (e.g., trade restrictions, asset freezes, prohibitions on financial transactions). For the purposes of this question, “economic sanctions” must restrict economic exchange (commercial or financial). Purely immigration/visa measures (e.g., tourist visa policy) are excluded unless they explicitly include commercial or financial prohibitions.
- Tariff: A tax or duty imposed on imported goods (or exports), typically paid by the importer, used to regulate foreign trade or protect domestic industry. For this question, “tariff measures” are instruments that impose or increase duty rates applicable to goods of the other country’s origin.

Authoritative publication channels (potential resolution sources):
- United States: Federal Register (official daily journal for rules, notices, and presidential documents) ; Presidential executive orders (assigned numbers and published in the Federal Register).
- Colombia: Diario Oficial (official publication of the Colombian State where laws, decrees, and official acts are published).

Why this question is interesting: After a near-miss on punitive trade measures in January, followed by diplomatic recalls in July and a high-profile U.S. visa revocation in late September, the odds of economically coercive steps (sanctions or tariffs) by either side before year-end are non-trivial yet uncertain.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and parties:
- Eligible actions must occur between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- “Either government” refers to the U.S. federal government and the national Government of Colombia (including the Presidency and national ministries/agencies). Actions by subnational entities (e.g., U.S. states, Colombian departments/municipalities) do not count.

What resolves YES:
The question resolves YES if, within the time window, at least one of the following occurs and is publicly verifiable:
A) A qualifying economic sanction is imposed or formally initiated that specifically targets the other country, defined as one of:
  - A prohibition or restriction on economic exchange with the other country’s government as an entity, or with classes of persons defined by nationality (e.g., “Government of Colombia” or “Colombian state-owned enterprises”; or, conversely, “Government of the United States” or “U.S. persons”), such as asset freezes or prohibitions on financial transactions.
  - An embargo or ban on imports from or exports to the other country, or sectoral restrictions explicitly limited to the other country.

B) A qualifying tariff measure is imposed or formally initiated that specifically targets the other country, defined as one of:
  - The imposition or increase of ad valorem or specific duty rates applicable to goods of the other country’s origin (across-the-board or product-specific), via a legally operative instrument (e.g., U.S. presidential proclamation, agency rule/notice; Colombian decree or resolution).

For both A and B, “formally initiated” means the measure is established by a legally operative instrument signed/issued within the window (even if its effective date is later), such as:
  - United States: a presidential executive order , presidential proclamation, or agency action/notice published in the Federal Register.
  - Colombia: a presidential decree, ministerial resolution, or tax/customs resolution published in the Diario Oficial.
A mere verbal statement of intent without an official legal instrument does not count.

What does NOT count:
- Measures not specific to the other country (e.g., global sanctions or tariffs that apply to many countries absent a specific carve-out naming the other country).
- Routine trade-remedy case steps (e.g., antidumping/countervailing investigations or preliminary determinations) unless the legally operative instrument explicitly frames the measure as a sanction or retaliatory tariff targeting the other country.
- Purely immigration/visa measures, recall/expulsion of diplomats, consular service changes, deportation-flight logistics, or administrative inspection slowdowns not codified as sanctions or tariffs.
- Actions adopted before 2025-10-15 UTC unless reissued as a new legal instrument within the window.

Evidence required to resolve:
- Primary preference: Official publications or documents, such as entries on federalregister.gov (U.S.) , signed executive orders , or Colombian decrees/resolutions in the Diario Oficial.
- If official publications are temporarily inaccessible, credible reporting that directly cites or links to such official acts (e.g., Reuters, AP) is acceptable.

Additional rules:
- If a qualifying measure is imposed/initiated within the window but later suspended or rescinded, the outcome remains YES (the measure occurred).
- If both governments take qualifying actions, the market resolves YES.
- If no qualifying action occurs within the window, resolve NO.

Notes for forecasters:
- Baseline: January’s threatened U.S. penalties were not imposed following a deal. Tensions escalated mid-year with reciprocal recalls  and a U.S. visa revocation announcement in late September.
- The CTPA (in force since 2012) provides a liberalized baseline; any new tariffs or sanctions specifically aimed at the other country would mark meaningful deterioration.

question: By December 31, 2025 (23:59:59 UTC), will the FOMC target range for the federal funds rate be 3.75%–4.00% or lower?
background:
Definitions and context
- Federal funds rate: The interest rate at which depository institutions lend reserve balances to other depository institutions overnight on an uncollateralized basis. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets a target range for this rate, typically expressed with lower and upper bounds (e.g., 0.00%–0.25%).
- FOMC: The committee within the Federal Reserve System responsible for U.S. monetary policy, including decisions about interest rates and the growth of the money supply; it sets the short‑term objective for open market operations, usually a target level/range for the federal funds rate.

Status quo (as of late September 2025)
- On September 17, 2025, the FOMC voted to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 4%–4¼%. The accompanying Implementation Note directs the Desk to undertake open market operations as necessary to maintain the federal funds rate in a target range of 4% to 4¼%, and it set the interest on reserve balances (IORB) rate at 4.15%, effective September 18, 2025.
- In the Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) released with the September 16–17, 2025 meeting, the median projection for the year‑end 2025 federal funds rate (defined as the midpoint of the projected appropriate target range) is 3.6%. The SEP explicitly notes that these projections refer to the midpoint of the target range at the end of the specified year.
- The next regularly scheduled year‑end policy meeting is on December 16–17, 2025, and is associated with a SEP, per the Federal Reserve’s posted FOMC calendar.

Why this question is non‑trivial
- The current target range is 4%–4¼% following the September decision , while the September SEP median implies a level around 3.6% (midpoint) by end‑2025. Reaching 3.75%–4.00% or lower by December 31, 2025 would require at least one additional policy action relative to the current setting, which is plausible but uncertain given incoming data and the FOMC’s dual mandate.
resolution_criteria:
Timing and scope
- Start date: October 1, 2025, 00:00:00 UTC.
- End date: December 31, 2025, 23:59:59 UTC.
- This question resolves based on the target range for the federal funds rate that is in effect at 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. Earlier changes are relevant only insofar as they determine the range in effect at the cutoff.

What counts as the “target range”
- Use the range explicitly stated by the Federal Reserve (e.g., “in a target range of X to Y percent”). This phrasing appears in official FOMC communications such as press releases and Implementation Notes (e.g., “target range of 4 to 4‑1/4 percent”).

Resolution rule
- Resolve Yes if, as of 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, the FOMC’s stated target range is exactly 3.75%–4.00% or any lower range (e.g., 3.50%–3.75%, 3.25%–3.50%, etc.).
- Resolve No if the target range is 4.00%–4.25% or any higher range (e.g., 4.25%–4.50%, 4.50%–4.75%, etc.).

Source of truth and how to verify
- Primary source: the Federal Reserve Board’s official monetary policy press release/statement and/or Implementation Note for the most recent FOMC action governing the target range in December 2025, as published on federalreserve.gov. For reference, the September 17, 2025 FOMC press release states the range change and the Implementation Note specifies the operational directive and IORB, illustrating the exact language used to define the range.
- If multiple FOMC actions occur in December 2025, use the last action whose effective range is in force as of 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. If no action occurs in December, use the latest prior action still in force as of the cutoff. The December 16–17, 2025 meeting is scheduled and is associated with a SEP, which is when a year‑end decision is typically made.

Notes
- Do not use market rates (e.g., the effective federal funds rate) to resolve this question; only the officially stated target range in FOMC communications is relevant.
- For definitional clarity on the federal funds rate and the FOMC’s role, see.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (inclusive), will the United States cast a veto in the UN Security Council on any draft resolution that explicitly calls for an immediate ceasefire in the Gaza Strip?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: On 2025-09-18, during the Security Council’s 10,000th meeting, a draft resolution that demanded an immediate, unconditional, and permanent ceasefire in Gaza received 14 votes in favour and 1 against (the United States) but was not adopted due to the negative vote by a permanent member (i.e., a veto). UN News likewise reported that the United States “once again vetoed a UN resolution demanding an immediate, unconditional and permanent ceasefire in the Gaza Strip,” and noted this was the sixth such US veto related to Gaza ceasefire texts, with the prior veto in June. These sources are indicative of the official documentation and media coverage used to verify Security Council voting outcomes and the language of the draft resolutions.

Key definitions and references for forecasters:
- United Nations Security Council veto: On non-procedural (substantive) decisions, any of the five permanent members (P5) can block adoption by casting a negative vote; procedural matters are not subject to veto; adoption otherwise requires at least nine affirmative votes. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_veto_power.
- Ceasefire: A temporary stoppage of fighting; synonymous terms include “truce” and “cessation of hostilities”. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceasefire.
- Gaza Strip: A Palestinian territory commonly referred to as “Gaza”. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip.

Primary sources for resolution: Security Council official meeting coverage and press releases (press.un.org) and UN News (news.un.org) typically report vote tallies and whether a draft “was not adopted owing to the negative vote of a permanent Council member,” as well as the operative language (e.g., “immediate ceasefire”). Major wire services (e.g., Reuters, AP) usually corroborate such votes; however, the official UN meeting coverage is the intended primary source for resolution verification.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone: The eligible period runs from 2025-10-15 00:00:00 to 2025-12-31 23:59:59, inclusive, in Eastern Time (America/New_York).

Question restated precisely: Resolve “Yes” if, during the above window, the United States (i.e., the permanent member of the UN Security Council representing the United States of America) casts a veto on any UN Security Council draft resolution that explicitly calls for an immediate ceasefire in the Gaza Strip. Resolve “No” otherwise.

What counts as a “veto”: For the purposes of this question, a veto means a negative vote by the United States on a non-procedural draft resolution that results in the draft not being adopted, as recognized in official UN Security Council meeting coverage (e.g., language that the draft “was not adopted owing to the negative vote of a permanent Council member”) or as shown by a voting record with at least nine votes in favour and the United States voting against. Abstentions or absences do not constitute a veto. Procedural matters are excluded.

What counts as “explicitly calls for an immediate ceasefire in the Gaza Strip”:
- The draft resolution’s operative text must include the word “immediate” modifying one of the following terms referring to the stoppage of fighting: “ceasefire,” “cessation of hostilities,” or “truce,” and must specify that this applies to Gaza/the Gaza Strip. Example qualifying language (non-exhaustive): “demands an immediate ceasefire in the Gaza Strip,” “calls for an immediate cessation of hostilities in Gaza,” “demands an immediate truce in the Gaza Strip.” The geographic reference may be phrased as “Gaza,” “the Gaza Strip,” or equivalent formulations that unambiguously refer to the Gaza Strip.
- Drafts lacking the word “immediate” in connection with the ceasefire/cessation/truce (e.g., “durable ceasefire,” “lasting ceasefire,” or “toward a ceasefire” without “immediate”) do not qualify.

Inclusions and exclusions:
- Include any such draft regardless of who sponsors it, provided it is voted on by the Security Council as a non-procedural matter within the time window.
- Exclude procedural votes, amendments voted separately from the main draft, presidential statements (PRSTs), press statements, General Assembly resolutions, and any texts whose ceasefire language is limited to areas outside Gaza or does not include “immediate.”
- If multiple qualifying drafts are vetoed by the United States in the window, any single instance suffices for “Yes.” If the United States votes against but there are fewer than nine votes in favour (so the draft fails without a veto), that does not count.

How it will be resolved (sources and method):
- Primary source: the official UN Security Council meeting coverage/press release for the relevant meeting(s) on press.un.org. The resolver will verify (a) that the United States cast a negative vote, (b) that the draft was not adopted owing to the negative vote of a permanent member, and (c) that the draft’s operative text explicitly called for an immediate ceasefire (or immediate cessation of hostilities/truce) in Gaza, as reflected in the UN’s description of the draft.
- Secondary confirmation (if needed): UN News coverage summarizing the vote and language (news.un.org). If discrepancies arise, the UN’s official meeting coverage/record takes precedence.
- In edge cases where the exact operative phrasing is not quoted in press coverage, the resolver will rely on the UN’s meeting coverage characterization (e.g., “demanding an immediate ceasefire in Gaza”) and, if available, the circulated draft text number referenced in the UN materials.

Decision rule: Resolve “Yes” if all three conditions are met within the time window: (1) the US cast a negative vote; (2) the draft failed due to the US veto; (3) the draft explicitly called for an immediate ceasefire (or immediate cessation of hostilities/truce) in Gaza as defined above. Otherwise resolve “No.”

question: Will the U.S. federal funds rate target range upper bound be at or below 3.75% at 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025?
background:
Why this matters: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets a target range for the U.S. federal funds rate, a key short-term policy rate that influences borrowing costs across the economy, including commercial and residential real estate financing. Lower policy rates generally reduce interest expenses and can support transaction volumes and valuations, which is directly relevant for real estate market activity.

Definitions and context:
- Federal funds rate: The interest rate at which depository institutions lend balances to each other overnight; see overview (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_funds_rate).
- FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee): The Fed body that sets the target range; overview (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Open_Market_Committee).
- Target range upper bound: The “high” endpoint of the FOMC’s target range for the federal funds rate; the Fed publishes a historical table with “Low” and “High” values and effective dates (https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/fedexplained/accessible-version.htm).
- DFEDTARU: The Federal Funds Target Range – Upper Limit series on FRED, expressed in percent per annum, typically shown at a daily frequency and sourced from the Board of Governors (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU).
- UTC: Coordinated Universal Time for timestamps (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time).

Status quo (for forecasting baseline): Assumption for this prompt only—verify independently. As of 2025-09-22, the most recent FOMC decision in mid-September 2025 set the target range to 4.00%–4.25%, implying DFEDTARU = 4.25%. Forecasters should confirm the latest value on FRED and the Fed’s table before making forecasts.

Why the 3.75% threshold: This cut-off aims to center probabilities for late-2025 outcomes, making the question non-trivial and sensitive to the number and timing of any further FOMC changes in Q4 2025.
resolution_criteria:
Start and end of measurement window:
- Start date/time: 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC (events before this are out of scope for interpretation, but only the end-date level determines resolution).
- End timestamp for evaluation: 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

What is being measured:
- The FOMC target range upper bound (“High” endpoint) of the U.S. federal funds rate at the evaluation timestamp defined above. This is the policy rate’s upper bound, not the effective federal funds rate (EFFR) published by the New York Fed.

Primary resolution source (use this first):
- FRED series “Federal Funds Target Range – Upper Limit” (DFEDTARU): https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU. Retrieve the observation with date 2025-12-31. If that observation is present, use its value (percent per annum) to resolve:
  • YES if DFEDTARU ≤ 3.75
  • NO if DFEDTARU > 3.75

Fallbacks if the primary source is unavailable, lacks a 2025-12-31 observation, or shows a clear data error:
1) Board of Governors “FOMC’s target range for the federal funds rate” table: https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/fedexplained/accessible-version.htm. Identify the row whose effective date/time makes the published “High” value in force at 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. Resolve based on that “High” value (YES if ≤ 3.75, else NO).
2) If further confirmation is needed, use the most recent FOMC statement/press release setting the target range that is effective at the evaluation time, available at: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy.htm (navigate to the relevant FOMC press release). Use the high end of the announced target range.

Time-zone and intra-day changes:
- If the FOMC implements a change on 2025-12-31 with a specific effective time, interpret that effective time in U.S. Eastern Time and convert to UTC to determine whether it is in force at 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-12-31.
- If multiple changes occur on 2025-12-31 (rare), use the level in force at 23:59:59 UTC.

Revisions and data discrepancies:
- If DFEDTARU or Fed table values are revised after 2025-12-31, use the value as displayed when resolving on or immediately after the close of 2025-12-31 UTC (within 7 calendar days). If primary and fallback sources conflict, prefer the Board of Governors table; if unavailable, use the latest applicable FOMC press release.

Clarifications:
- Do not use the Effective Federal Funds Rate (EFFR) for resolution; only the target range upper bound applies.
- Units are percent per annum, unrounded. If the source displays with two decimals, use the displayed precision.
- This question resolves definitively to YES or NO based on the value determined above.

question: Will Congress enact a law by December 31, 2025 that extends the enhanced ACA premium tax credits (ARPA/IRA enhancements to IRC §36B) to any tax year beyond 2025?
background:
Summary of the status quo (as of 2025-09-30):
• What the enhanced ACA premium tax credits (ePTCs) are: ePTCs are the temporary American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA; P.L. 117-2) changes to the Affordable Care Act’s Premium Tax Credit (PTC) under Internal Revenue Code §36B, later extended by the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA; P.L. 117-169) through the end of tax year 2025. ARPA: (1) eliminated the 400% Federal Poverty Level (FPL) income cap for PTC eligibility, and (2) replaced the applicable percentage schedule to lower required premium contributions, which for households at or above 400% FPL effectively caps the benchmark contribution at 8.5% of income. The IRA extended these ARPA provisions for tax years 2023–2025.
• What the underlying Premium Tax Credit (PTC) is: The PTC is a refundable, advanceable tax credit under IRC §36B designed to help eligible individuals and families afford insurance purchased on the ACA marketplaces (exchanges). Key terms used in PTC calculations include Federal Poverty Level (FPL), the benchmark plan (second-lowest-cost silver plan in the rating area), and the applicable percentage schedule that caps the required premium contribution as a share of income.
• Expiration timing: Under current law, the ARPA/IRA ePTC enhancements sunset after December 31, 2025 (i.e., they apply through tax year 2025). Independent health-policy analysis confirms the IRA extension through 2025 and discusses impacts if ePTCs expire after 2025.
• Legislative and fiscal context heading into Q4 2025: On September 19, 2025, the U.S. Senate rejected a House-passed stopgap funding bill (continuing resolution) that would have funded federal agencies through November 21, 2025, by a 44–48 vote, highlighting uncertainty over near-term legislative vehicles. As of September 26, 2025, the Congress.gov FY2026 Appropriations Status Table shows no FY2026 appropriations bills enacted (no Presidential Approval dates listed), underscoring that year-end negotiations could include health policy riders. One current legislative effort specifically aimed at extending the ePTCs is H.R. 5145 (119th Congress), titled the “Bipartisan Premium Tax Credit Extension Act”.

Definitions and links for forecasters:
• Affordable Care Act (ACA): Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patient_Protection_and_Affordable_Care_Act.
• Internal Revenue Code (IRC) §36B: The statutory section establishing the PTC; general overview in CRS report.
• Federal Poverty Level (FPL): HHS poverty guidelines used in PTC calculations; defined in CRS  and at https://aspe.hhs.gov/topics/poverty-economic-mobility/poverty-guidelines.
• Benchmark plan (second-lowest-cost silver plan): The premium used in the PTC formula; defined in CRS.
• Enhanced ACA premium tax credits (ePTCs): The ARPA/IRA temporary modifications to IRC §36B that (i) eliminate the 400% FPL eligibility cap and (ii) implement a revised applicable percentage schedule that lowers required premium contributions (including the 8.5% cap at ≥400% FPL for benchmark premiums), in effect for tax years 2021–2025.

Why this question has non-trivial uncertainty: Whether Congress uses a late-2025 legislative vehicle (e.g., omnibus appropriations or a negotiated health package) to extend the ARPA/IRA PTC enhancements beyond 2025 is actively contested, with meaningful partisan and fiscal trade-offs and multiple plausible pathways (or failure) before year-end.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone:
• Eligible enactments must occur between 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. Resolution will be determined at or shortly after 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

What counts as “extends the enhanced ACA premium tax credits beyond 2025” (for this question):
• The law must explicitly continue the ARPA/IRA enhanced PTC regime under IRC §36B for any tax year after 2025 (e.g., 2026 or later). For this question, “enhanced PTC regime” means BOTH of the following ARPA/IRA features remain in effect under IRC §36B beyond tax year 2025: (i) elimination of the 400% FPL income cap for PTC eligibility; and (ii) retention of the ARPA applicable percentage schedule that lowers required premium contributions (including the 8.5% of income cap for households at or above 400% FPL for benchmark plan premiums).
• Partial extensions that do not include both elements above (e.g., an extension that removes the subsidy cliff but does not retain the ARPA applicable percentage schedule, or vice versa) resolve as No.
• Administrative or regulatory actions (e.g., agency guidance) do not count; only enactment of a federal statute that amends or extends the relevant provisions of IRC §36B counts.

Operational resolution rule:
• Resolve Yes if, by 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, a federal statute has been enacted (signed by the President and assigned a Public Law number) and the statutory text shows the ARPA/IRA enhanced PTC features defined above continue to apply to any tax year beyond 2025 (i.e., the sunset is moved or removed for those features). Primary source: Congress.gov bill status page showing “Became Public Law” and the Public Law text (on Congress.gov or GovInfo) reflecting the extension. Secondary cross-checks (not determinative) may include reputable health policy trackers such as KFF.
• Resolve No if no such Public Law is enacted by the deadline, or if any enacted law extends only a subset of the enhancements such that both features defined above are not retained beyond 2025.

Clarifications:
• “Public Law” means a law enacted by Congress and signed by the President or enacted over a veto; the presence of a Public Law number and “Became Public Law” status on Congress.gov will be used to confirm enactment by the deadline. If the President signs the bill but Congress.gov has not yet updated the status by the deadline, the GovInfo publication of the Public Law or authoritative White House release can be used to confirm enactment.
• The extension must apply nationally to the IRC §36B PTC and is not satisfied by pilot programs or temporary administrative actions.
• The ACA, PTC under IRC §36B, FPL, benchmark plan definitions are as in CRS sources cited above.

Sources for resolution and background claims:
• CRS on ePTC expiration and ARPA/IRA features.
• KFF analysis confirming extension through 2025 and impacts of expiration.
• Reuters reporting on the Sept. 19, 2025 Senate rejection of a CR.
• Congress.gov FY2026 Appropriations Status Table indicating no FY2026 appropriations enacted as of Sept. 26, 2025.
• Congress.gov page for H.R. 5145 (119th Congress) titling the “Bipartisan Premium Tax Credit Extension Act”.

question: Will the EPA’s final 2027 total renewable fuel volume be at least 24.0 billion RINs by December 31, 2025?
background:
The U.S. Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) requires the EPA to set annual volume requirements for four categories of renewable fuel, including “total renewable fuel,” via notice-and-comment rulemaking. In the last finalized “Set 1” rule, EPA set the 2025 total renewable fuel requirement at 22.33 billion RINs (one RIN equals one ethanol‑equivalent gallon).

As of 2025-09-22, EPA has proposed “Set 2” standards for 2026–2027 with total renewable fuel volumes of 24.02 billion RINs (2026) and 24.46 billion RINs (2027), docket EPA‑HQ‑OAR‑2024‑0505. On 2025-09-16, EPA issued a supplemental proposed rule addressing small refinery exemptions and related reallocations; these remain proposals pending a final rule.

Final RFS rules are published in the Federal Register; the 2026–2027 action’s proposed rule was published there on 2025-06-17. This question asks whether the final rule, if published by 2025‑12‑31, will set the 2027 “total renewable fuel” applicable volume at ≥24.0 billion RINs.
resolution_criteria:
Start date/time: 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC. End date/time: 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

YES if, on or before the end date, the EPA publishes in the Federal Register a FINAL rule for the Renewable Fuel Standard that specifies the 2027 “total renewable fuel” applicable volume at 24.0 billion RINs or higher. “Total renewable fuel” refers to the RFS program category encompassing all qualifying renewable fuel; “RIN” means Renewable Identification Number, the compliance credit used in RFS; 1 RIN equals one ethanol-equivalent gallon.

Primary resolution source: the Federal Register publication of the final rule setting 2026–2027 RFS standards (Docket EPA‑HQ‑OAR‑2024‑0505), as displayed on federalregister.gov (use the “Publication Date” field to determine timeliness). If the final rule expresses the 2027 total renewable fuel volume in gallons rather than RINs, convert using 1 RIN = 1 ethanol‑equivalent gallon. Compare the published 2027 total renewable fuel applicable volume to the 24.0 billion RIN threshold without rounding (i.e., 24.00 billion = 24,000,000,000 RINs).

NO if no such final rule is published by the end date/time, or if a final rule is published by the deadline but sets the 2027 total renewable fuel applicable volume below 24.0 billion RINs. If multiple final-rule documents affecting the 2027 total renewable fuel volume are published within the window (e.g., corrections), use the most recent final publication within the window. Subsequent litigation or stays after publication do not affect resolution.

question: U.S. 30-year mortgage rate: Will Freddie Mac’s PMMS show ≥ 6.50% for the last weekly 30‑year FRM average published in December 2025?
background:
Overview and definitions
- Primary Mortgage Market Survey (PMMS): Freddie Mac’s long‑running weekly survey that reports national average mortgage rates. Since November 2022, PMMS averages are computed from loan application data submitted to Freddie Mac’s Loan Product Advisor and are limited to first‑lien, conventional, conforming, fully amortizing purchase mortgages for borrowers with 20% down (LTV ~80%) and excellent credit (e.g., ≥740 FICO), for owner‑occupied single‑family properties in the contiguous U.S..
- Publication cadence and dating: PMMS is published weekly, typically on Thursdays at 12:00 p.m. ET. If a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, PMMS publishes on the Wednesday of that week. The PMMS “week” covers applications from 12:00 a.m. ET Thursday through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Entries are dated by the publication date (e.g., “September 25, 2025”). 
- Where to find the data: Freddie Mac maintains public archives listing weekly 30‑Year Fixed‑Rate Mortgage (30‑Yr FRM) averages by date. These pages display the rate to two decimal places and clearly show the weekly dates (e.g., Sep 11, 18, 25, 2025). The current‑week snapshot is also shown on the Mortgage Rates landing page.

Status quo as of late September 2025
- As of the PMMS publication dated September 25, 2025, the 30‑year FRM averaged 6.30%.
- Recent weekly readings in September 2025 have been in the mid‑6% range, including 6.26% (Sep 18) and 6.35% (Sep 11) per the archive. Some weeks have touched 6.50% (e.g., Sep 4, 2025).

Why this matters for forecasting
- The late‑year outcome depends on macroeconomic data, Federal Reserve policy guidance, and mortgage‑Treasury spread dynamics. With recent PMMS readings around the mid‑6% range and occasional prints at 6.50%, whether the final December 2025 weekly publication lands at or above 6.50% remains uncertain enough to support non‑trivial forecasting.

Key terms (for clarity)
- “30‑Year FRM average” refers to the national average interest rate (not APR) for the 30‑year fixed‑rate mortgage series reported by PMMS, as defined by Freddie Mac’s methodology in effect at the time of publication.
- “Publication date” is the date shown on the PMMS archive entry for that weekly release (e.g., “December 24, 2025” or “December 31, 2025”), which follows the cadence described above.
resolution_criteria:
How this question resolves
- Scope: Consider all PMMS weekly publications with a publication date between 2025‑12‑01 00:00 ET and 2025‑12‑31 23:59 ET, inclusive. Identify the weekly publication with the latest publication date within that window (“the last weekly PMMS publication dated in December 2025”). Note: PMMS is typically published Thursdays at 12:00 p.m. ET, and if that Thursday is a U.S. holiday, publication occurs on Wednesday of that week.
- Metric used: For that last December 2025 publication, take the “30‑Yr FRM” Average Rate value as displayed on the Freddie Mac PMMS archive page (no additional rounding by the resolver; use the value as shown to two decimal places).
- Resolution rule: Resolve “Yes” if that displayed 30‑Yr FRM Average Rate is greater than or equal to 6.50%. Resolve “No” if it is below 6.50%.
- Source of truth: The Freddie Mac PMMS archive pages that list the weekly 30‑Yr FRM averages and publication dates. Acceptable sources include: https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms/archive and/or https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms/pmms_archives. If multiple official Freddie Mac pages present the weekly rate for the same date, the PMMS archive(s) take precedence over press releases or third‑party sites.
- Edge cases: If, contrary to normal practice, no PMMS weekly publication is dated in December 2025, resolve this question as “No.” This preserves a definite binary outcome while relying on the PMMS publication cadence as documented.

question: By 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, will the most recent eligible public IAEA publication between October 15 and December 31, 2025 report Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched to (up to) 60% U‑235 as at least 460.0 kilograms (U mass)?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01
- Latest known level: A confidential IAEA report seen by Reuters on September 3, 2025 stated that Iran’s stock of uranium enriched to up to 60% U‑235 was 440.9 kg as of June 13, 2025. An independent analysis of the same IAEA report specifies the figure as 440.9 kg (U mass) as of June 13, 2025 and lists other enrichment-category stockpiles, consistent with IAEA reporting conventions. Reuters also characterized 60% enrichment as close to “weapons grade”.
- IAEA access/inspection status: In his September 8, 2025 introductory statement to the Board of Governors, the IAEA Director General said the Agency halted verification activities during June attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities and withdrew inspectors by the end of June due to safety concerns; as of early September, the Agency had not had access to verify Iran’s high-enriched uranium for almost three months and was negotiating modalities to resume inspections. The IAEA chronology confirms public statements and briefings on Iran in September 2025.
- UN “snapback” context: The reimposition (“snapback”) of UN sanctions on Iran was completed on September 27, 2025 at 8:00 p.m. EDT, reactivating prior Security Council resolutions; the process had been initiated on August 28, 2025, and involved France, Germany, and the United Kingdom.
- IAEA publication channels and cadence: The IAEA publicly posts the Director General’s Iran-related Board reports (GOV documents) and related verification/monitoring documents on its “IAEA and Iran – IAEA Board Reports” page, which serves as a central repository for these reports and indicates a roughly quarterly reporting rhythm; the page links directly to PDFs of current-year reports. The IAEA also posts Director General statements and news releases on iaea.org.

Key definitions (for clarity in this forecast)
- Uranium-235 (U‑235): A fissile isotope of uranium that constitutes about 0.72% of natural uranium and is the target of enrichment.
- Enriched uranium: Uranium with a higher mass percentage of U‑235 than natural uranium (0.72%); low-enriched uranium (LEU) is <20% U‑235; highly enriched uranium (HEU) is ≥20% U‑235 (percentages by mass).
- “U mass”: In IAEA reporting and technical analyses, stockpiles are often expressed as kilograms of uranium (element-only), excluding other elements in chemical compounds (e.g., fluorine in UF6). The September 2025 analysis of the IAEA report denotes the 60% stockpile as “kg (U mass),” reflecting this convention; IAEA enrichment percentages are specified by mass.
- “Uranium enriched to (up to) 60% U‑235” (the “60% category”): The phrasing used by IAEA and media summaries refers to uranium whose U‑235 assay is reported at or near 60% (commonly stated as “up to 60% U‑235”). For this question, references to “60%,” “up to 60%,” or “60 percent U‑235” are treated as referring to this category as presented by IAEA publications.

Why this is forecastable now
- As of June 13, 2025, Iran’s 60% stockpile stood at 440.9 kg (U mass). Subsequent access interruptions, evolving cooperation, and the September 27, 2025 UN snapback reimposition create uncertainty about stockpile trajectory through Q4 2025. IAEA typically produces at least one public report/statement in Q4, enabling an up-to-date figure to be available before year-end. The 460.0 kg threshold is close enough to the last known level to make both outcomes plausible.

Where to find the resolution source
- IAEA and Iran – IAEA Board Reports (for GOV documents on safeguards and verification/monitoring): https://www.iaea.org/newscenter/focus/iran/iaea-and-iran-iaea-board-reports 
- IAEA Director General statements and IAEA News Center (for public statements/news releases that may include quantified figures): https://www.iaea.org/newscenter/statements/ and https://www.iaea.org/news.
resolution_criteria:
Question
- Resolve Yes if, by 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, the most recent eligible IAEA publication in the defined window reports Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched to (up to) 60% U‑235 as ≥460.0 kilograms (U mass). Otherwise resolve No.

Eligible publications (all must be met)
- Source: An official, publicly accessible IAEA item on iaea.org in one of these categories: (a) IAEA Director General report (GOV document) linked on the “IAEA and Iran – IAEA Board Reports” page; or (b) an official IAEA news release or Director General statement posted on iaea.org that includes a quantified figure for Iran’s 60% stockpile.
- Publication window: Published on iaea.org (visible publication date on the item’s page) between 00:00:00 UTC on 2025-10-15 and 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-12-31, inclusive.
- Content: Explicitly contains a single quantified figure for the total stockpile of uranium enriched to (up to) 60% U‑235, expressed in kilograms. If both “kg” and “(U mass)” are provided, use the “kg (U mass)” value. If only “kg” is provided and context indicates stockpiles are reported as uranium mass, treat it as kg (U mass). If only non-metric units are given, convert to kilograms using 1 lb = 0.45359237 kg and use that numeric value for comparison.

“Most recent” rule
- If multiple eligible items exist, use the one with the latest publication date-time shown on iaea.org. If two eligible items share the same publication date-time, use the one with the latest last-updated timestamp if shown; if still tied, use the item with the higher document number (e.g., later GOV/2025/XX). If timestamps are not shown, treat the date as the determinant.

Counting the 60% figure
- Qualifying text includes “uranium enriched to 60%,” “enriched up to 60% U‑235,” or equivalent IAEA phrasing for the 60% category. Use the explicitly stated total for that category. Do not sum subcomponents unless the IAEA item explicitly provides a total or unambiguously indicates that the listed components are additive and exhaustive; if only partial components are listed and no total is given, the item is not eligible and should be skipped.

Numeric comparison
- Compare the stated (or converted) number to the threshold: Yes if ≥460.0 kg; No if <460.0 kg. Use the numeric value printed in the IAEA item without attempting to adjust for measurement uncertainty or implied rounding. If a range is given, use the midpoint. If only qualitative language is used (e.g., “around 460 kg”) but a numeric value appears, use the numeric value as printed.

Edge cases and fallbacks
- If no eligible IAEA item (as defined above) is published in the window that contains a quantified 60% stockpile figure, resolve No (verifiable by absence on the IAEA Board Reports page and IAEA statements/news pages).
- If an eligible item is published but is later corrected/updated before the resolution deadline, use the latest version as of 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

Definitions and references (for clarity)
- Uranium-235 (U‑235): fissile isotope; ~0.72% of natural uranium.
- Enriched uranium and HEU/LEU thresholds are defined by mass percent U‑235.
- “U mass” denotes uranium element mass; IAEA enrichment percentages and stockpile figures are given by mass; September 2025 reporting/analysis explicitly uses “kg (U mass)” for the 60% stockpile.

Status-quo citations for forecasters
- 60% stockpile at 440.9 kg (U mass) as of June 13, 2025.
- IAEA inspector withdrawal and paused access in June; verification of high-enriched uranium overdue as of early September.
- UN sanctions snapback completed September 27, 2025 at 8:00 p.m. EDT.
- IAEA publicly posts Iran Board reports and DG statements/news on iaea.org (central repository and September 2025 examples).

question: Will the year-over-year change in BEA’s Core PCE price index for November 2025 be at least 2.8%?
background:
Definition and series: The "Core PCE price index" refers to the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index excluding food and energy, published by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). BEA describes this series and displays its "Change From Month One Year Ago" (i.e., the 12‑month percent change) on its data page for the PCE price index excluding food and energy. This series is part of BEA’s monthly Personal Income and Outlays release.

Release timing and availability: BEA’s public release schedule lists "Personal Income and Outlays, November 2025" as a news release on December 23, 2025 at 8:30 AM (U.S. ET), ensuring the November 2025 figure is available before year‑end. As a reference for typical wording and timing, the August 2025 news release shows how BEA states the 12‑month percent changes for headline PCE and for PCE excluding food and energy and notes the next release timing (e.g., "October 31, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. EDT").

Status quo: Recent core PCE 12‑month percent changes shown by BEA include June 2025: +2.8%, July 2025: +2.9%, and August 2025: +2.9%. The August 2025 news release states: "Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 2.9 percent from one year ago". These recent values provide context for the November 2025 forecast.

Why this question: Core PCE is the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge. Setting the threshold at 2.8% targets a range where informed forecasters can reasonably disagree based on trends, energy pass‑throughs, shelter components, and goods disinflation, while still resolving cleanly via a single authoritative source.
resolution_criteria:
Start and end of eligibility window: This question concerns the November 2025 reference month and will resolve based on data published between 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC.

Primary metric: The "year-over-year change" is the 12‑month percent change that BEA labels "Change From Month One Year Ago" for the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index excluding food and energy. "At least 2.8%" means greater than or equal to 2.8%.

Resolution source and priority: Use the BEA as the sole source of truth. Resolve using the value for November 2025 reported in the "Personal Income and Outlays, November 2025" news release and/or its associated data tables hosted on bea.gov, which are scheduled for publication on December 23, 2025. If the news release text and tables differ, use the numeric value in the BEA release tables for November 2025.

Exact resolution rule: Resolve YES if BEA’s reported 12‑month percent change for the PCE price index excluding food and energy (core PCE) for November 2025 is greater than or equal to 2.8%. Resolve NO if it is strictly less than 2.8%.

Precision and rounding: Use the figure exactly as displayed by BEA on the release page/tables at the time of publication within the eligibility window. Do not apply any additional rounding beyond what BEA displays.

Revisions: If BEA revises the November 2025 figure after initial publication but before 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC, use the latest figure displayed by BEA within that window. Any revisions posted after that cutoff are ignored.

Links and examples: BEA’s release schedule page where the "Personal Income and Outlays, November 2025" entry appears is at bea.gov/news/schedule. BEA’s data page defining and displaying the PCE price index excluding food and energy and its "Change From Month One Year Ago" is at bea.gov/data/personal-consumption-expenditures-price-index-excluding-food-and-energy. The August 2025 Personal Income and Outlays news release illustrates BEA’s standard phrasing for the 12‑month percent change measures.

question: Between 00:00 UTC on Oct 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on Nov 30, 2025, will at least three new named storms be first officially named by the National Hurricane Center in the Atlantic basin?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- Official season window and typical late-season activity: The Atlantic hurricane season officially runs from June 1 to November 30, with most activity between mid-August and mid-October. Typical formation dates for later-season storms still extend into October–November (e.g., the 13th named storm typically forms by Oct 25 and the 14th by Nov 19).
- 2025 seasonal outlook (updated Aug 7, 2025): NOAA’s update kept the season tilted above normal, calling for 13–18 named storms, 5–9 hurricanes, and 2–5 major hurricanes, and characterizing the overall odds as 50% above-normal, 35% near-normal, 15% below-normal.
- 2025 season-to-date: As of 03 UTC on Sep 30, 2025, the North Atlantic summary listed 9 named storms, 3 hurricanes, and 3 major hurricanes; ACE ~83.2 (x10^4 kt^2). The NHC 2025 advisory archive lists named storms to date including Andrea, Barry, Chantal, Dexter, Erin, Fernand, Gabrielle, Humberto, and Imelda.
- Definitions and conventions used for this question: NHC defines a Tropical Storm as a tropical cyclone with maximum sustained 1-minute winds of 34–63 kt, and a Subtropical Storm as a subtropical cyclone with maximum sustained winds of 34 kt or more. NHC advisories are issued in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) and include the official advisory time in the header (e.g., 0300Z, 0900Z, 1500Z, 2100Z). For geographic scope, the Atlantic basin consists of the North Atlantic Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, and the Gulf of Mexico.
Primary resolution source: NHC’s 2025 Tropical Cyclone Advisory Archive (Atlantic) will be used to identify each named system and the UTC time of the first advisory where the system is first named as a Tropical Storm or Subtropical Storm , applying the UTC conventions documented by NHC.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Between 00:00:00 UTC on 2025-10-15 and 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-11-30 (inclusive), will at least three (3) new named storms be first officially named by the National Hurricane Center (NHC) in the Atlantic basin?

Operational definition of terms:
- Atlantic basin: The North Atlantic Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, and the Gulf of Mexico.
- Named storm (for counting): A tropical or subtropical cyclone that receives an official name from NHC when it first attains Tropical Storm or Subtropical Storm intensity (i.e., maximum sustained 1-minute surface winds of at least 34 kt), as reflected in NHC advisory products. We rely on NHC’s definitions of Tropical Storm and Subtropical Storm.
- First officially named time: The UTC timestamp of the earliest NHC advisory in the 2025 archive for that cyclone in which the cyclone is first referred to as “Tropical Storm [Name]” or “Subtropical Storm [Name]”. Use the advisory header time shown in the archived product (UTC). If the first naming occurs in a “Special Advisory” or “Intermediate Advisory,” that product’s UTC header time is used.

Counting rules:
- Include a cyclone if and only if its first officially named time (as defined above) falls between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-11-30 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive.
- Systems that formed earlier as disturbances or depressions but are first named within the window count; systems first named before the window do not count even if they strengthen within the window.
- Count each unique cyclone at most once. Renaming of the same cyclone does not occur in the Atlantic basin under normal NHC practice; if an exceptional renaming occurred, only the first naming time is considered.
- “Potential Tropical Cyclone” advisories, tropical depressions, post-tropical cyclones, and extratropical cyclones that never receive a tropical or subtropical storm name do not count.

Resolution procedure (to be executed on or after 2025-12-01 UTC and no later than 2025-12-31 UTC):
1) From the NHC 2025 Tropical Cyclone Advisory Archive, open the Atlantic section and list all named cyclones for 2025.
2) For each candidate cyclone, open Advisory Number 1 and any earlier “Special” or “Intermediate” advisories if present, and identify the earliest advisory where the system is first referenced as “Tropical Storm [Name]” or “Subtropical Storm [Name]”. Record that advisory’s UTC header time.
3) Count how many cyclones have a first officially named time within the inclusive window 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC to 2025-11-30 23:59:59 UTC.
4) Resolve “Yes” if the count is ≥ 3; otherwise resolve “No”.

Primary sources:
- NHC 2025 Tropical Cyclone Advisory Archive (Atlantic) for names and advisory times.
- NHC advisory time conventions and UTC usage.

Notes:
- This market resolves based on the operational advisory archive as posted on nhc.noaa.gov. Any subsequent post-season reanalysis that modifies best-track genesis/naming times does not affect resolution, which is tied to the archived advisory header times.
- All dates/times are in UTC.

Status quo context (non-binding for resolution):
- Official Atlantic season dates and typical late-season formation timing.
- NOAA’s Aug 7, 2025 update maintained above-normal probabilities and 13–18 named storms.
- Through 03 UTC Sep 30, 2025, there were 9 named storms listed in the North Atlantic summary; the 2025 advisory archive lists nine named storms to date.

question: Will ACMA publicly find that Optus breached at least one emergency-call-related rule for the 18 September 2025 Triple Zero outage by 31 December 2025?
background:
Context and status quo (as of 2025-09-30):
- Triple Zero (000) is Australia’s primary national emergency telephone number for police, fire, or ambulance, and the emergency call service is regulated at the federal level. The Department of Infrastructure notes that the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) regulates and monitors the provision of the emergency call service under the Emergency Call Service Determination and related law. ACMA’s public guidance describes how Triple Zero works and when to use it.
- On 18 September 2025, Optus experienced an outage affecting Triple Zero access. On 22 September 2025, ACMA announced it had commenced an investigation into Optus’s compliance with emergency call service regulations and other related rules for that incident, and said it will make its findings public once the investigation concludes. In that statement, ACMA cited three specific instruments and described the obligations in scope: (1) Telecommunications (Emergency Call Service) Determination 2019 (e.g., ensure emergency calls are successfully carried; undertake welfare checks on callers who made unsuccessful emergency calls during a significant network outage; notify the Emergency Call Person (Telstra) as soon as possible of a significant network outage), (2) Telecommunications (Customer Communications for Outages) Industry Standard 2024 (e.g., put up-to-date outage information on websites and communicate with customers via channels such as apps, email, SMS, media or call centres; notify specified stakeholders including the relevant ministerial department, the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman, the National Emergency Management Agency and the ACMA), and (3) Communications Alliance Industry Code C536: Emergency Call Service Requirements.
- ACMA’s summary of the Emergency Call Services Determination 2019 highlights key obligations, including maintaining emergency call networks and facilities, notifying Emergency Call Persons (ECPs) and other providers of significant outages, and conducting welfare checks on individuals who tried to call during a large network outage.
- Precedent: Following the nationwide Optus outage on 8 November 2023, ACMA determined that Optus breached emergency call rules by failing to provide access to Triple Zero for 2,145 people and failing to conduct 369 welfare checks; ACMA announced penalties totaling more than A$12 million on 8 November 2024.

Definitions used in this question:
- ACMA: The Australian Communications and Media Authority.
- Optus: Singtel Optus Pty Limited and/or its subsidiaries, as referenced by ACMA in its enforcement actions (e.g., ACMA’s 2024 announcement concerning “subsidiaries of Singtel Optus Pty Limited (Optus)” ). Any ACMA finding that any such Optus group entity contravened/breached the specified instruments counts for this question.
- Triple Zero (000): Australia’s primary national emergency number and emergency call service as described by the Department of Infrastructure and ACMA public materials.
- Emergency-call-related rules/obligations (for the purposes of this market): The obligations set out in any of the following instruments, to the extent they relate to emergency call carriage or to mandated actions during/after outages affecting emergency call access: (a) Telecommunications (Emergency Call Service) Determination 2019; (b) Telecommunications (Customer Communications for Outages) Industry Standard 2024; (c) Communications Alliance Industry Code C536: Emergency Call Service Requirements. These are the instruments ACMA explicitly cited as being in scope for the 18 September 2025 outage investigation. For accessible descriptions of ECSD 2019 obligations, see ACMA’s public explainer.
- Emergency Call Person (ECP): For Australia’s 000/112 service, the ECP is Telstra; ACMA’s statement refers to notifying “the emergency call person (Telstra)” about significant outages.

Why this is forecastable now: ACMA has opened an investigation and stated it will publish findings when concluded, but as of 2025-09-30 the outcome is not yet known. Prior precedent shows ACMA has made breach findings and issued penalties in a similar context (the 2023 outage), yet timelines and facts could differ, making a year-end publication uncertain.
resolution_criteria:
YES if, between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC inclusive, ACMA publishes on the acma.gov.au domain an official item (e.g., media release, article/news post, investigation outcome/report, decision/notice) that explicitly states that Optus (Singtel Optus Pty Limited and/or its subsidiaries) breached, contravened, or failed to comply with at least one of the following, in relation to the 18 September 2025 Triple Zero outage: (a) Telecommunications (Emergency Call Service) Determination 2019; (b) Telecommunications (Customer Communications for Outages) Industry Standard 2024; or (c) Communications Alliance Industry Code C536: Emergency Call Service Requirements. The ACMA’s 22 Sep 2025 statement confirms these instruments are in scope for the investigation.

- The publication must clearly link the breach/contravention/failure to comply to the 18 September 2025 outage (e.g., “in relation to the Triple Zero outage on 18 September 2025”).
- Acceptable wording includes ACMA stating that Optus “breached,” “contravened,” or “failed to comply with” any of the listed instruments; examples of such language are used by ACMA in prior enforcement (e.g., “failed to provide access to the emergency call service,” “failed to conduct welfare checks”).
- The publication date/time used for eligibility is the date/time shown on the ACMA page (acma.gov.au) in UTC-equivalent; if only a local timestamp is shown, convert to UTC for assessment.

NO if no such ACMA publication exists by the end of the eligibility window, or if ACMA publishes only interim updates, statements of ongoing investigation, or materials that do not clearly state a breach/contravention/failure to comply tied to the 18 September 2025 outage and one of the listed instruments. Publications about different incidents or dates, or about entities other than Optus (as defined above), do not count.

Primary resolution sources to check (non-exhaustive examples):
- ACMA’s dedicated statement on the Optus Triple Zero investigation (for context on the instruments and scope; final outcome will be published by ACMA when concluded).
- ACMA’s news/articles and media releases sections at acma.gov.au.
- Any ACMA investigation outcome, enforcement decision, or infringement notice page on acma.gov.au that explicitly states an Optus breach/contravention for the 18 Sep 2025 outage and cites one of the listed instruments.

Notes:
- If ACMA simultaneously publishes across multiple ACMA pages, any one qualifying page is sufficient.
- Third-party media reports alone do not qualify; the decisive evidence must be on acma.gov.au. If the ACMA site is temporarily unavailable but the same page is accessible via an official government web archive (e.g., National Library of Australia/Internet Archive snapshot of the acma.gov.au page), the archived ACMA page may be used for resolution as long as its content and timestamp clearly meet the above criteria.
- This market does not require ACMA to issue penalties; a clear ACMA finding of a breach/contravention/failure to comply is sufficient, as per the language ACMA used in the 2023 outage penalties announcement.

question: Will the United States impose a triple‑digit (≥100%) ad valorem tariff on PRC‑origin imports between 05:01 UTC on November 10, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: In spring 2025, the U.S. briefly imposed triple-digit tariffs on many Chinese-origin goods (about 145%), which sharply reduced seaport imports, before a truce lowered rates. Following negotiations announced May 12, 2025, the U.S. reduced extra tariffs on China to 30% from 145%, while China cut to 10% from 125% for a 90-day period. On August 12, 2025, the U.S. extended this tariff truce by an additional 90 days, preventing the immediate reversion to triple-digit duties; the extension runs until 12:01 a.m. EST on November 10, 2025 (05:01 UTC).
